Xeriscapes can reduce [ water consumption ](/wiki/Water_consumption "Water
consumption") by 60% or more compared to regular lawn landscapes.  [12]  In
Turkey, one of the first large scale xeriscaping evaluations was conducted. It
was found that switching an average city park to more native vegetation in the
region can lower irrigation usage by 30–50%. Assuming a water usage reduction
of 30% it was found that a city can save roughly $2 million annually (however,
this exact value is dependent on location).  [13]  The use of native plants
lowers the necessity of watering as the vegetation has already adapted to
thrive in the climate and does not require assistance with irrigation or
fertilization.

The [ Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design
](/wiki/Leadership_in_Energy_and_Environmental_Design "Leadership in Energy
and Environmental Design") program has recognized xeriscaping as an effective
water reduction process and has started to incorporate credits in the
certification process across all their programs for facilities that reduce
their outside water use and irrigation. This credit can be met by using
xeriscape strategies and efficient irrigation systems.  [14]  This further
validates the beneficial claims behind xeriscaping, and it is anticipated that
more energy and environmental credit systems as well state ran programs will
encourage and incentivize xeriscaping for greenspace development.  [13]  [15]

While evaluating the cost of annual maintenance and park construction,
xeriscaping drastically lowers these costs by roughly 55% and 57%,
respectively.  [13]  Aside from occasional [ weeding ](/wiki/Weeding
"Weeding") and [ mulching ](/wiki/Mulching "Mulching") , xeriscaping requires
far less time and effort to maintain.  [16]  This is the case because under
xeriscaping principles the vegetation used for urban greenspaces are
indigenous to the area; therefore, are less expensive and require less
assistance to acclimate and survive in the environment when compared to
imported vegetation. This means that the systems use less water as well as
lower rates of pesticides, and [ fertilizers ](/wiki/Fertiliser "Fertiliser")
when compared to current urban and residential greenspaces; this further helps
lower annual maintenance costs.  [13]  Furthermore, maintenance waste, such as
lawn clippings, contribute organic waste to landfills and fertilizers
contribute to [ urban runoff ](/wiki/Urban_runoff "Urban runoff") [ pollution
](/wiki/Pollution "Pollution") ; however, xeriscaping eliminates these
negative effects as clippings are encouraged to remain on the greenspace which
allows for a lower use of fertilizers.  [17]

**Sewage Treatment Systems in Victorian-Era London**  

The transformation of London’s sanitation infrastructure during the Victorian era stands as one of the most significant public health achievements of the 19th century. Prior to these developments, the city’s waste disposal relied heavily on cesspits and the direct discharge of sewage into the River Thames, practices that contributed to repeated outbreaks of cholera, typhoid, and other waterborne diseases. The construction of integrated sewer networks under the guidance of pioneering engineers marked a turning point in urban hygiene and set new standards for municipal water treatment worldwide.  

**Early Conditions and Public Health Crisis**  
By the mid-1800s, London’s population had expanded rapidly, far outpacing the capacity of its antiquated waste management systems. Human and industrial waste accumulated in open drains and waterways, with the Thames serving both as a source of drinking water and a receptacle for effluent. The resulting contamination was linked to devastating cholera epidemics in 1832, 1849, and 1854, each claiming thousands of lives. Public awareness of the connection between polluted water and disease was heightened by the work of physician John Snow, whose investigation into the 1854 Soho cholera outbreak provided compelling evidence for waterborne transmission.  

**Engineering Leadership: Joseph Bazalgette and the Metropolitan Board of Works**  
The most notable figure in London’s sewage reform was Sir Joseph Bazalgette, appointed chief engineer of the Metropolitan Board of Works in 1856. Tasked with designing a system to intercept and divert sewage away from the Thames, Bazalgette conceived a network of large, brick-lined interceptor sewers running parallel to the river. These conduits collected waste from existing smaller sewers and conveyed it downstream, away from central London, for discharge into tidal stretches where dilution was greater.  

Bazalgette’s design incorporated over 1,300 miles of street sewers feeding into 82 miles of main interceptors. The system was complemented by massive pumping stations—most famously at Crossness and Abbey Mills—that lifted sewage from low-lying areas into the gravity-fed network. The scale of construction was unprecedented, requiring millions of bricks, Portland cement, and innovative techniques for tunneling beneath densely built districts.  

**Construction and Implementation**  
Work commenced in earnest following the “Great Stink” of 1858, when hot weather intensified the odor from the Thames, prompting Parliament to approve extensive funding for Bazalgette’s plan. Construction proceeded over the next decade, with careful attention to gradients, ventilation, and structural durability. The main interceptors were built with egg-shaped cross-sections, a design that improved flow velocity and reduced sediment deposition.  

By 1875, the majority of London’s sewage was being conveyed through the new system and discharged downstream of the city’s water intakes. Although initial treatment was minimal—relying largely on dilution and tidal flushing—the relocation of waste outfalls had an immediate impact on reducing contamination of drinking water sources.  

**Public Health Outcomes**  
The completion of the interceptor network corresponded with a marked decline in cholera and other waterborne diseases in London. While improvements in water filtration and supply also contributed, the removal of raw sewage from central stretches of the Thames was a decisive factor. The engineering works demonstrated the value of large-scale infrastructural investment in combating urban epidemics and became a model emulated by other industrial cities.  

**Legacy and Influence**  
Bazalgette’s sewers remain in operation today, integrated into modern treatment systems that include sedimentation tanks, biological processing, and chemical disinfection. The Victorian network’s durability attests to the foresight in materials and construction methods. Moreover, the project underscored the interplay between civil engineering and public health policy, illustrating how technical solutions could address widespread social problems.  

In the broader historical context, London’s Victorian sewer system represents a pivotal chapter in environmental engineering. It bridged the gap between rudimentary waste disposal and the scientifically informed treatment processes of the 20th century, laying the groundwork for contemporary urban sanitation standards. The success of these efforts not only improved quality of life but also demonstrated the transformative power of infrastructure in shaping the health and sustainability of cities.

**Microsoft Tests Underwater Data Center Off Scottish Coast to Boost Efficiency and Sustainability**  

In June 2018, Microsoft announced a bold step in its ongoing quest to improve data center performance and sustainability: the deployment of a self-contained, submarine-like capsule housing a complete data center beneath the waters off the Orkney Islands in Scotland. The initiative, part of the company’s Project Natick, was designed to explore the potential of an underwater environment to enhance cooling efficiency, extend hardware longevity, and streamline maintenance, while leveraging renewable energy sources to reduce the carbon footprint of operations.  

The Orkney Islands location was chosen for its unique combination of cool ocean temperatures and abundant renewable energy. The region’s grid is powered entirely by wind, solar, and tidal generation, providing an ideal testbed for Microsoft’s goal of operating data centers with minimal environmental impact. The capsule, measuring roughly 12.2 meters in length, was constructed to withstand the pressures and conditions of the seabed while housing 864 servers and associated cooling infrastructure.  

**Cooling Efficiency and Hardware Durability**  
One of the most significant challenges facing traditional land-based data centers is thermal management. High-performance computing generates substantial heat, requiring extensive cooling systems that consume large amounts of electricity. By situating the facility underwater, Microsoft harnesses the naturally low temperatures of the surrounding seawater to dissipate heat more efficiently. This passive cooling approach reduces reliance on mechanical chillers and air conditioning units, cutting energy use and potentially lowering operational costs.  

In addition to cooling benefits, the sealed capsule protects hardware from airborne contaminants, humidity fluctuations, and temperature swings typical of terrestrial environments. The absence of human traffic inside the data center minimizes the risk of accidental damage and dust accumulation, factors that can degrade equipment over time. Engineers anticipate that the controlled, stable conditions of the underwater setting will extend the lifespan of components and reduce the frequency of replacements.  

**Maintenance and Operational Logistics**  
Project Natick’s design philosophy emphasizes minimal maintenance. The underwater capsule is intended to operate autonomously for up to five years without direct human intervention. Remote monitoring systems track performance, temperature, and other critical metrics, while redundancy in server architecture ensures continued operation even if individual units fail.  

Deployment and retrieval are handled using specialized marine vessels and equipment, enabling the capsule to be installed or removed relatively quickly compared to building or decommissioning a traditional data center. The modular nature of the design also means that additional capsules could be positioned in coastal regions where renewable energy and suitable marine conditions align.  

**Environmental and Carbon Footprint Considerations**  
By combining passive seawater cooling with a renewable-powered grid, the Orkney test site serves as a proof of concept for low-emission, high-efficiency data centers. Conventional facilities often rely on fossil-fuel-generated electricity and energy-intensive cooling, contributing to significant greenhouse gas emissions. Microsoft’s underwater model demonstrates how alternative siting and design approaches can mitigate these impacts.  

Moreover, the project aligns with broader industry trends toward sustainable technology infrastructure. As demand for cloud computing and digital services grows, data centers are projected to consume increasing amounts of energy. Innovative solutions like Project Natick could play a role in meeting this demand without proportionally expanding the sector’s environmental footprint.  

**Future Prospects**  
The success of the Orkney deployment will inform Microsoft’s decisions about scaling the underwater data center concept. Researchers are collecting data on energy consumption, server performance, and environmental impact to evaluate the feasibility of commercial rollouts. Potential applications include providing computing capacity to coastal cities, supporting remote communities, and serving industries that require robust, low-latency connections.  

While the underwater approach may not replace traditional data centers entirely, it represents a novel addition to the array of strategies available for sustainable computing infrastructure. By integrating location-specific advantages—such as cool marine environments and renewable energy grids—into design, companies can explore new ways to balance performance, cost, and environmental responsibility.  

Microsoft’s experiment beneath the Scottish waves is as much about reimagining the physical form of data centers as it is about improving their efficiency. If successful, Project Natick could mark the beginning of a shift toward more diverse, adaptive, and ecologically conscious models for housing the digital backbone of modern society.

**Cutting Energy Costs at Home with Smart Technology: A Practical Guide**  

For many households, monthly utility bills are a constant reminder of how much energy modern living demands. The good news is that recent advances in smart home technology offer practical ways to cut those costs—without sacrificing comfort or convenience. By combining automation, energy-efficient appliances, and well‑planned usage schedules, homeowners can achieve noticeable savings while reducing their environmental footprint.  

### Automating for Efficiency  

Smart home automation isn’t just about convenience; it’s about precision. Devices such as smart plugs, connected thermostats, and intelligent lighting systems allow you to control when and how energy is used. For example, a smart thermostat can learn your daily routine and adjust heating or cooling accordingly—warming the house just before you wake, then lowering the temperature while you’re away. Motion‑activated lighting ensures that rooms aren’t illuminated unnecessarily, and smart plugs can disable standby power draw from electronics when not in use.  

Automation also enables remote control, meaning you can turn off appliances or adjust settings from your phone. This prevents waste when plans change and you’re away longer than expected. Over time, these small adjustments add up to significant savings.  

### Choosing Energy‑Efficient Appliances  

While automation optimizes usage, it’s equally important to start with appliances that consume less energy in the first place. Look for products with ENERGY STAR certification or equivalent efficiency ratings. Modern refrigerators, washing machines, and dishwashers often use far less electricity and water than older models.  

Pairing these appliances with smart features enhances their efficiency further. For instance, some washing machines can be programmed to run at off‑peak hours, and dishwashers may include eco‑modes that lower water temperature and reduce consumption without compromising cleaning performance. Upgrading may require an initial investment, but the long‑term savings in utility costs often offset the expense.  

### Optimizing Power Usage Schedules  

Energy providers frequently offer time‑of‑use pricing, where rates vary depending on demand. Smart home systems make taking advantage of these schedules straightforward. By programming appliances to operate during off‑peak hours—such as running laundry cycles at night or charging electric vehicles in the early morning—you can reduce costs substantially.  

Smart energy monitors can track usage patterns in real time, helping you identify which devices consume the most power and when. This data empowers you to make informed decisions: shifting high‑energy activities to cheaper time slots, or spreading them out to avoid spikes.  

### Integrating Systems for Maximum Impact  

The true potential of smart home technology lies in integration. When devices communicate with one another through a central hub or app, they can coordinate actions that multiply savings. For instance, a smart thermostat can signal window sensors to close blinds on hot afternoons, reducing cooling needs. Lighting systems can dim automatically when natural daylight is sufficient, and appliances can delay operation until solar panels are producing optimal output.  

By linking automation, efficient appliances, and thoughtful scheduling, households can establish a self‑regulating energy ecosystem. This not only lowers bills but also supports sustainability goals.  

### Getting Started  

For those new to smart home energy management, begin with a single focus area—such as heating and cooling, which often accounts for the largest portion of household energy use. Install a smart thermostat, monitor results for a few months, then expand to lighting, appliances, and other systems.  

Gradual implementation allows you to learn how each device works and understand its impact, ensuring that every addition delivers measurable benefits. Over time, the combination of automation, efficiency, and scheduling will transform your home into a model of cost‑effective energy use.  

**Conclusion**  

Reducing household energy costs is no longer limited to turning off lights or lowering the thermostat manually. With smart technology, it’s possible to automate habits, choose appliances that inherently use less energy, and strategically schedule power usage—all without compromising daily comfort. The integration of these approaches creates a streamlined, intelligent home environment that saves money and supports a more sustainable future.

**Strawbale Houses in Rural France: Cultural History and Architectural Significance**  

Strawbale construction occupies a distinctive place in the architectural heritage of rural France, particularly in regions where cereal agriculture has long been a primary economic activity. The practice, which saw its earliest documented uses in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, combines locally available organic materials with vernacular building traditions, producing dwellings that are both functional and culturally emblematic. This entry examines the historical context, construction techniques, decorative practices, and the preservation of strawbale houses as part of France’s rural heritage.  

---

**Historical Context**  
In the agrarian landscapes of northern and western France, straw—chiefly from wheat, rye, and barley—was an abundant byproduct of harvest. Traditionally used for thatching, animal bedding, and composting, surplus straw also found structural application in building. The introduction of mechanical balers in the late 19th century enabled the production of compact, uniform bales, which could be stacked and bound to form walls. This innovation coincided with a period of rural self-sufficiency, when farmers often built their own homes using readily available materials. Strawbale houses thus emerged as a cost-effective alternative to stone or timber construction, especially in areas with limited access to quarried rock or mature forests.  

---

**Construction Techniques**  
The fundamental principle of strawbale construction is the use of densely packed bales as infill within a supporting frame or, in some cases, as load-bearing walls. In rural French examples, frames were typically made from softwood timbers, often oak or chestnut in older structures, set upon a stone or brick plinth to elevate the straw above ground moisture.  

Bales were stacked in running bond patterns, with vertical stakes or wooden pins driven through to enhance stability. Openings for windows and doors were framed with timber lintels and jambs, ensuring load distribution away from vulnerable sections. Once the bale walls were in place, they were coated with a protective layer—traditionally a lime-based plaster—which served both as weatherproofing and as a breathable barrier, allowing moisture to escape while preventing rain penetration. Interior finishes varied from plain limewash to more elaborate decorative painting, reflecting local tastes and available pigments.  

---

**Decorative Styles and Regional Variations**  
While strawbale houses were often utilitarian in form, certain regions developed distinctive decorative traditions. In Brittany, for instance, lime-plastered exteriors might be tinted with ochre or iron oxides, producing warm earthy tones. In parts of Normandy, decorative timber framing was integrated into the façade, with plaster infill concealing the straw core. Interiors could feature hand-painted motifs, floral stencils, or simple geometric designs, especially in parlors or main living spaces.  

Roofing materials also contributed to regional identity: thatched roofs remained common in western coastal areas, while clay tiles or slate were favored inland. The combination of strawbale walls and traditional roofing created a harmonious aesthetic, blending the house into its agricultural surroundings.  

---

**Role in Preserving Local Heritage**  
Today, surviving strawbale houses are valued not only for their resource-efficient construction but also for their cultural resonance. They embody a period of rural ingenuity, when communities relied on seasonal abundance to meet architectural needs. Preservation efforts often focus on maintaining the original materials and building techniques, with skilled artisans applying lime plaster repairs and replacing damaged bales using traditional methods.  

In some villages, restored strawbale houses serve as museums or cultural centers, offering visitors insight into historical farming practices and sustainable building. They also contribute to the broader narrative of French vernacular architecture, which encompasses a diverse range of materials and methods adapted to local climates and economies.  

---

**Conclusion**  
Strawbale houses in rural France represent a synthesis of practicality, environmental adaptation, and regional artistry. Their construction reflects an intimate relationship between agricultural life and domestic architecture, while their preservation supports the continuity of local heritage. As living examples of sustainable building long before modern ecological movements, they offer a tangible link to the past and a model for resource-conscious design in the present.

### !41856big.jpgWhat is short rotation coppice? Some fast growing tree species can be cut down to a low stump (or stool) when they are dormant in winter and go on to produce many new stems in the following growing season. This practice is well established in the UK and Europe, having been a traditional method of woodland management over several hundred years for a variety of purposes including charcoal, fencing and shipbuilding. ### Suitable species A number of different species are suitable for coppicing, with different optimum cycle periods. In the UK many different species have been coppiced in the past, however the principal species currently used for SRC for biomass for energy are: ## SRC willow ### Varieties Willow ( _Salix_ spp.) is planted as rods or cuttings in spring using specialist equipment at a density of 15,000 per hectare. The willow stools readily develop multiple shoots when coppiced and several varieties have been specifically bred with characteristics well suited for use as energy crops. Information and advice is available from the Forest Research Yield models for energy coppice of poplar and willow website. ### Growth During the first year it can grow up to 4 m in height, and is then cut back to ground level in its first winter to encourage it to grow multiple stems. The first harvest is in winter, typically three years after cut back, again using specialist equipment, however a cycle of 2 or 4 to 5 years is also common. In fertile sites growth can be very strong during the first two years after coppicing, giving rapid site capture, reducing thereafter and so a 2-year cutting cycle may be more appropriate. ### Yield Yield is dependent on many factors, including: - Site - Water availability - Weed control - Planting density - Light - Temperature. ### Harvesting Typically the first harvest may be expected to be somewhat lower than subsequent ones, and figures from 7 to 12 oven dried tonnes per hectare per annum can be expected on reasonably good sites. Harvesting may be as rods (up to 8 m length), billets (5-15 cm lengths) or as direct chip harvesting. Direct chip harvesting can cause problems for storage with rapid composting (and hence loss of energy content) and mould formation (and attendant health risks) owing to the high moisture content of freshly harvested willow. This can be less of a problem with billets owing to improved air flow through the pile. ### Viability A willow SRC plantation may be expected to be viable for up to 30 years before it becomes necessary to replant and can reach 7-8 m in height at harvest. The site should be reasonably flat, or with a slope no more than 7% and, to be eligible for the Defra Energy Crops Scheme (ECS) grant, needs to be at least 3 ha, though this need not all be in a single plot. ## SRC Poplar ### Growth Poplar ( _Populus_ spp.) displays more apical dominance than willow and is therefore less ready to develop multiple stems following coppicing. Shoots can reach up to 8 m by the end of the first rotation. It therefore tends to develop fewer, thicker stems than willow, and consequently has a lower bark to wood ratio. Individual shoots can reach up to 8 m by the end of the first 3-year rotation. ### Planting Poplar is planted in spring, from cuttings. These cuttings must have an apical bud within 1 cm of the top of the cutting. Because of this it is difficult to use poplar in equipment developed for planting willow short rotation coppice. Planting density is lower than for willow, typically 10-12,000 per ha. Cut back takes place late in the following winter. ### Yield Yield is very site dependent, and in some sites can outperform willow. Average yield on a suitable site is likely to be in the region of 8 oven dry tonnes per hectare per year. ### Harvesting Poplar responds well to harvesting cycles of around four or five years which is slightly longer than the 3 years often recommended for willow. This is because growth in the first year following cutback or harvest is generally not as rapid as in subsequent years. Combined with a very up right growth habit this means that the crop may not develop a closed canopy, and hence maximum light interception, until the second or third year. Harvesting requires similar equipment to willow, however, owing to the tendency of poplar to form fewer, heavier stems, it must be slightly more robust. Removal of a poplar crop at the end of the useful life of the plantation can be more difficult than for willow as poplar often forms a large taproot which will generally require a large excavator to remove or more time to decay naturally. ## Broadleaf coppice Many traditional broadleaf species can be grown as coppice, such as ash, hazel, sweet chestnut, sycamore, etc. The rotation is typically longer than for willow or poplar, and the yield is lower, but for management within a mixed woodland this can both help to produce products on a more regular basis than from conventional forestry, and also may be useful to produce smaller diameter logs and stems for both firewood and traditional coppice markets.

# Affnan’s Excellent Aquaponics Siphon Posted by Ecofilms on Jan 17, 2011 in Aquaponics, DIY Aquaponics \| 2 comments ### !Affnan Ramli Since Malaysian Affnan Ramli began tinkering with Aquaponics a few years ago in his small backyard, he has successfully managed to redesign and simplify one of the central pieces of kit used in Aquaponics – The Auto-Siphon. Affnan runs a very successful blog where he constantly shares you-tube clips of his system designs and generously shares his experiences in Aquaponics. We caught up with him recently to to tell us a little more about his innovative siphon. ### How did you first find about Aquaponics? For a long time I’ve been doing ornamental fish keeping, mostly Goldfish, Koi and Gouramis. From there, I began experimenting on Bio filters to reduce work needed in maintaining fish ponds. It then further evolved to water gardening as one way to reduce Nitrates in pond water. With numerous research on water gardening on the net – it brought me to Aquaponics. At the time this was a new term for me. Further reading on subject and with a lot of research on the net mostly to Australian sites I feel this is a perfect system for my small backyard. ### How difficult was it to build your first system? In March 2008 without much experience and virtually no clear instruction available on how to go about it, I started to build my first system out of 1 x 3 containers and using 15mm straight stand pipe as siphon. I had no idea this is too small at the time. ### What mistakes did you make along the way? Numerous failures, nothing significant grew and most plants died after few weeks. Those that survived are nothing to be proud off. Reliable water control is the main issue; it’s too unpredictable the siphon to be effective or dependable. Usual siphon problem either it’s don’t start leaving high water or don’t stop causing low water level in the grow beds, killing either the plants or the fish. ### Affnan’s Siphon Explained !Affnan's Bell Valve The Affnan Siphon is based around the work of fluid dynamics and 18th Century Dutch/Swiss mathematician Daniel Bernoulli. He created Bernoulli’s Principal, which roughly states that an increase in the speed of the fluid occurs simultaneously with a decrease in pressure or a decrease in the fluid’s potential energy. This insight was used by Affnan in designing his aquaponics siphon. What Affnan did was attach a larger funnel to the top of his up-stand pipe. As a larger volume of water rushes into a constricted space it creates enough pressure to drive the siphon action. A simple idea that simplifies the construction of an auto-siphon in aquaponics. Read more about building your own Affnan Siphon Here ### Your siphon that you helped improve and develop is commonly referred to as the Affnan Siphon by many people here in Australia. Can you tell us how you developed and designed it? After about 8 months of trial and error with various designs to make siphon more reliable I arrive at the present siphon. My main criteria on a design are simplicity, ease of maintenance and reliability. We cannot afford to have something that can fail without understanding why it fails, so that we have a reliable Aquaponics system. I have made minor improvement on its outlet to cater for my “high water” level in my fish tank. I constantly monitor the siphon and look at feed back from users, to address any problem that may come after usage. To date nothing major has been done. Most failure is due to plants roots, algae growth and significant reduction in pump capacity. These issues are external and can be resolve by routine cleaning of the siphon. [](http://www.ecofilms.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2011/01/Affnan-Valve-1.jpg) ### How hard is it to find plumbing parts in your country? I am making few sets for some friends, those parts needed use are common plumbing item over here. It will take me 5 minutes the most in any hardware store that I walk into to get those parts. ### What are the common reasons why a lot of people have difficulty with getting their siphons to flow properly? This is a very difficult question to answer. Water flow in a Siphon must not be too restrictive or within the siphon having steps than could cause excessive back flow. The mechanics of siphon although look simple but its fluid dynamic that need to be looked at. An ideal siphon will have a smooth funnel that can channel water giving maximum effect for a good siphon (action). The whole siphon as an assembly, works to achieve this ideal siphoning. I understand many people having difficulties to get parts, but I would recommend understanding siphon principle on how to increase efficiency and overcome the equilibrium flow the its possible to use alternate parts to achieve the result. ### What tips do you have for people starting to build their siphon for the first time? The stand pipe and funnel combination get the best possible smooth flow. Ratio of stand pipe to funnel don’t exceed 1:2

**Rain in Motion: Sculptural Rooftops that Transform Stormwater into Public Art**  

Cities have long battled the challenge of stormwater management, but in recent years, a new approach has emerged—one that marries function with beauty. Decorative rooftop rainwater sculptures offer a way to guide precipitation away from overburdened infrastructure while simultaneously creating dynamic, interactive art installations. These designs invite residents to look upward during a rainstorm and witness their environment come alive with movement, sound, and light.  

### The Concept of Rooftop Water Sculpture  

At its core, a rooftop rainwater sculpture is an architectural feature integrated into a building’s roofline or gutter system. Instead of allowing rain to flow invisibly into downspouts, the sculpture channels water into visible pathways—spiraling chutes, cascading chains, or kinetic panels—that turn each rainfall into a performance. The water’s journey becomes part of the city’s visual language, reflecting seasonal changes and weather patterns.  

This concept draws inspiration from traditional Japanese *kusari-doi* (rain chains), which have long combined functional water diversion with aesthetic appeal. Contemporary interpretations expand on this idea, using modern materials, LED lighting, and even sound design to create multisensory experiences.  

### Design Elements for Urban Integration  

Successful rooftop rainwater sculptures balance artistry with practical engineering. Key considerations include:  

1. **Structural Support:** Sculptures must be securely anchored to withstand wind loads and the weight of flowing water. Stainless steel, powder-coated aluminum, and reinforced glass are common choices for durability.  

2. **Flow Dynamics:** Designers often model water movement using fluid simulation software to ensure smooth, uninterrupted flow. Curved channels and textured surfaces can influence the water’s speed and splash pattern.  

3. **Seasonal Adaptation:** In climates where freezing occurs, modular components allow for seasonal removal or transformation. Some installations switch to dry sculptures in winter, replacing water with reflective materials or light projections.  

4. **Integration with Existing Systems:** Sculptures can divert water into storage cisterns, green roofs, or rain gardens. While the primary goal is visual engagement, routing the water to sustainable endpoints enhances the installation’s environmental value.  

### Community Engagement Through Art  

One of the most compelling aspects of rooftop rainwater sculptures is their ability to foster community connection. In dense urban neighborhoods, where green space is scarce, these installations create moments of shared wonder. Residents may gather in courtyards or streets during storms to watch water dance down a sculptural facade.  

Public art festivals have begun to incorporate rainwater sculptures as interactive exhibits. For example, a downtown arts district might commission local artists to design rooftop features for several buildings, creating a “rain trail” that visitors can follow. During wet weather, the trail becomes an open-air gallery, with each rooftop offering a unique interpretation of the same natural event.  

### Case Studies in Creative Stormwater Design  

In Berlin, a mixed-use development integrated copper rain chains shaped like abstract leaves along its facade. As water flows, it produces a soft, metallic patter that resonates in the building’s atrium. Residents describe the sound as calming, turning rainy days into a sensory experience rather than an inconvenience.  

In Portland, Oregon, an artist collaborated with architects to build a rooftop installation featuring translucent panels etched with intricate patterns. Rainwater runs across the panels, magnifying the designs and refracting light into the surrounding streetscape. At night, embedded LEDs illuminate the flowing water, creating a luminous waterfall effect visible from blocks away.  

### Looking Ahead  

The future of decorative rooftop rainwater sculptures lies in combining artistry with smart technology. Sensors could measure rainfall and adjust lighting or sound accordingly, while augmented reality apps could overlay virtual elements onto the physical sculpture during storms. These innovations promise to deepen the connection between urban residents and the natural cycles around them.  

By reimagining rooftops as stages for rain’s performance, cities can turn a routine meteorological event into a source of inspiration. Whether through the shimmer of water on polished steel, the rhythm of droplets on ceramic, or the interplay of shadow and light, rooftop rainwater sculptures invite us to see our built environment not as a barrier to nature, but as a canvas for its most ephemeral beauty.

Americas

Cotton bolls discovered in a cave near [ Tehuacán
](/wiki/Tehuac%C3%A1n,_Puebla "Tehuacán, Puebla") , Mexico, have been dated to
as early as 5500 BC, but this date has been challenged.  [13]  More securely
dated is the domestication of _[ Gossypium hirsutum ](/wiki/Gossypium_hirsutum
"Gossypium hirsutum") _ in Mexico between around 3400 and 2300 BC.  [14]
During this time, people between the Río Santiago and the Río Balsas grew,
spun, wove, dyed, and sewed cotton. What they did not use themselves, they
sent to their Aztec rulers as tribute, on the scale of ~116 million pounds
annually.  [15]

In [ Peru ](/wiki/Peru "Peru") , cultivation of the indigenous cotton species
_[ Gossypium barbadense ](/wiki/Gossypium_barbadense "Gossypium barbadense") _
has been dated, from a find in Ancon, to  c.  4200 BC  ,  [16]  and was the
backbone of the development of coastal cultures such as the [ Norte Chico
](/wiki/Norte_Chico_civilization "Norte Chico civilization") , [ Moche
](/wiki/Moche_culture "Moche culture") , and [ Nazca ](/wiki/Nazca_culture
"Nazca culture") . Cotton was grown upriver, made into nets, and traded with
fishing villages along the coast for large supplies of fish. The Spanish who
came to Mexico and Peru in the early 16th century found the people growing
cotton and wearing clothing made of it.

## Types of Air Purifiers Different air purifiers work using a range of technologies. A few are helpful. Others are ineffective, or even potentially harmful to your health. **Mechanical filters:** These purifiers use fans to force air through a dense web of fine fibers that trap particles. Filters with very fine mesh are called HEPA filters, as described above. While they work on microscopic particles, they can also remove larger particles (including dust, pollen, and some mold spores) when they’re suspended in the air. (Some filters are labeled “HEPA-type” or “HEPA-like.” They haven’t been certified to meet the requirements of a true HEPA filter but may still perform adequately in our tests.) Mechanical filters don’t help with gases or odors. And they can be expensive. Mechanical filters need to be replaced every six to 12 months. Replacement filters usually cost less than $80, but some can cost more than $200. **Activated carbon filters:** Unlike mechanical filters, these filters use activated carbon to capture certain types of gases, including certain odor-causing molecules. But they’re not particularly effective against formaldehyde, ammonia, or nitrogen oxide. Because activated carbon filters don’t combat particles, many air purifiers will have both an activated carbon filter and a mechanical filter. Activated carbon filters get saturated faster than mechanical filters, though, and require replacement more frequently, every three months, as opposed to every six to 12 months for mechanical filters. Make sure to budget for replacements accordingly. Activated carbon filters usually cost up to $50 each. **Ozone generators:** These appliances produce ozone, a molecule that can react with certain pollutants to alter their chemical composition. This can result in dangerous indoor air quality, and CR doesn’t recommend this type of air purifier. Makers of ozone generators often claim that the devices emit safe levels of ozone, but our tests have found that even at low settings, some ozone generators quickly exceeded the Food and Drug Administration’s limit of 0.05 parts per million for medical devices. Plus, studies reviewed by the Environmental Protection Agency have shown that low levels of ozone don’t effectively destroy indoor pollutants. Ozone has also been linked to decreased lung function and increased risks of throat irritation, coughing, chest pain, and lung tissue inflammation. Exposure might also worsen asthma, emphysema, and bronchitis. **Electrostatic precipitators and ionizers:** With these electronic models, particles in the air become charged so that they stick—magnetlike—to plates on the machine or to nearby surfaces. CR doesn’t typically test electronic air purifiers, and we don’t recommend them because they can produce ozone. **Ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI):** Some manufacturers claim that their air purifiers kill airborne viruses, bacteria, and fungal spores with UV lamps. But they might miss certain bacteria and mold spores that are resistant to UV radiation. And for this method to be effective, the UV light must be powerful enough and the exposure must last long enough—minutes to hours, rather than the few seconds typical of most UVGI air purifiers. CR doesn’t test UVGI technology, though some mechanical air purifiers we test may have the added function. **Photocatalytic oxidation (PCO):** Some air purifiers use ultraviolet radiation and a photocatalyst, such as titanium dioxide, to produce hydroxyl radicals that oxidize gaseous pollutants. Depending on the pollutant, this reaction can generate harmful byproducts, such as ozone, formaldehyde, nitrogen dioxide, and carbon monoxide. CR doesn’t currently test air purifiers with PCO technology. There have been few field investigations exploring the effectiveness of PCO air purifiers, but one laboratory study, conducted by researchers at Syracuse University in New York, reported that the devices didn’t effectively remove any of the volatile organic compounds ( VOCs) typically found in indoor air. **Photoelectrochemical oxidation (PECO):** This variant of PCO emerged in 2017 from the manufacturer Molekule. The Molekule Air purifier didn’t score well in our tests for dust, smoke, and pollen removal. Since then, we’ve also tested the more expensive Molekule Air Pro, which performed better at removing contaminants on its highest setting but still didn’t impress in overall performance, nor did it rate well for reliability or owner satisfaction in our member survey.

Much like rain, snow and ice are very good at exacerbating existing road
defects because of the freeze-thaw cycle. When water gets into cracks it
freezes and expands, this puts pressure on the existing defect and makes it
bigger, weakening the surface over time until small cracks become large
potholes.

**The Flavor of Sustainability: Why Compost-Grown Vegetables Belong on Your Plate**  

When we talk about eating healthier, the conversation often centers on reducing processed foods, balancing macronutrients, and increasing fresh produce intake. But there’s a deeper layer to this story—how that produce is grown. Vegetables cultivated in soil enriched with compost not only support the environment but also can deliver superior nutrition and flavor. By choosing compost-grown vegetables from local organic farms, you can nourish your body while participating in a regenerative food system.  

### Nutritional Advantages of Compost-Grown Vegetables  

Compost is a natural soil amendment created from decomposed organic matter, rich in essential minerals and beneficial microorganisms. When incorporated into farm soil, compost improves structure, aeration, and water retention, fostering robust plant growth. Research has shown that vegetables grown in compost-rich soil often contain higher levels of certain micronutrients—such as magnesium, potassium, and antioxidants—compared to those grown in depleted or synthetically fertilized soils.  

The microbial diversity in composted soil also plays a role in nutrient bioavailability. Healthy soil microbiomes help plants absorb trace minerals more effectively, which can translate into more nutrient-dense food on your plate. For example, carrots grown in compost-amended beds have been found to contain elevated beta-carotene, while leafy greens can show increased vitamin C and iron content.  

### Sourcing from Local Organic Farms  

Local organic farms that use compost not only produce nutrient-rich vegetables but also reduce the environmental impact of food production. Buying directly from these farms cuts down on transportation emissions and supports regional agricultural economies.  

To find such farms, start by exploring your local farmers’ market. Ask vendors about their soil practices—many will be proud to share their composting methods and may even invite you to visit their fields. Community-supported agriculture (CSA) programs are another excellent option, offering weekly boxes of seasonal produce straight from compost-nourished soil.  

### Cooking with Compost-Grown Vegetables: Recipes to Try  

**1. Roasted Root Medley with Herb Oil**  
*Ingredients:*  
- 2 cups compost-grown carrots, sliced  
- 2 cups compost-grown beets, cubed  
- 1 tbsp olive oil  
- 1 tsp sea salt  
- Fresh rosemary and thyme  

*Toss the vegetables with olive oil, salt, and herbs. Roast at 400°F (200°C) for 35 minutes, until tender and caramelized. The natural sweetness of compost-grown root vegetables shines through in this simple preparation.*  

**2. Kale and Quinoa Power Salad**  
*Ingredients:*  
- 4 cups compost-grown kale, chopped  
- 1 cup cooked quinoa  
- 1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved  
- ½ cup toasted pumpkin seeds  
- Dressing: olive oil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, honey  

*Massage the kale with a touch of olive oil to soften the leaves. Combine with quinoa, tomatoes, and seeds. Whisk dressing ingredients together and drizzle over salad. The nutrient density of compost-grown kale makes this dish a powerhouse of vitamins and minerals.*  

**3. Summer Squash Stir-Fry**  
*Ingredients:*  
- 2 cups compost-grown zucchini, sliced  
- 1 cup compost-grown bell peppers, strips  
- 1 tbsp sesame oil  
- 2 cloves garlic, minced  
- Soy sauce to taste  

*Heat sesame oil in a wok, sauté garlic, then add vegetables. Stir-fry for 5–7 minutes until crisp-tender. Compost-grown squash often has a richer flavor profile, making this quick dish stand out.*  

### Tips for Making the Most of Your Compost-Grown Produce  

- **Store smartly:** Keep leafy greens in breathable bags to maintain freshness.  
- **Cook simply:** Minimal seasoning allows the natural flavors to shine.  
- **Preserve excess:** Freeze chopped vegetables or make pickles to enjoy them year-round.  

By intentionally choosing vegetables grown in compost-enriched soil, you elevate both your meals and your connection to the earth. Every bite becomes part of a cycle—where waste transforms into nourishment, and nourishment inspires healthier living.

# How Does Crystal Deodorant Work and Does It Have Any Side Effects? Medically reviewed by Alexandra Perez, PharmD, MBA, BCGP — Written by Emily Cronkleton — Updated on August 22, 2024 Crystal deodorant is a type of alternative deodorant made of natural mineral salt called potassium alum, also known as potassium aluminum sulfate. It has been shown to have antimicrobial properties. Potassium alum has been used as a deodorant in Southeast Asia for hundreds of years. Crystal deodorant has become more popular in Western cultures in the last 30 years. It has gained popularity due to its: - natural ingredients - low cost - purported health benefits, such as lowering the risk of breast cancer It’s widely believed that the absorption of aluminum and other harmful chemicals through the underarm can lead to breast cancer. However, according to the National Cancer InstituteTrusted Source, there are no scientific studies to support these claims. That said, some people still wish to eliminate unnecessary chemicals from their body products as much as possible. Scientific studies proving the advantages of crystal deodorant are lacking, and many of the benefits are anecdotal. Some people swear by it, while others swear it doesn’t work. It all comes down to a matter of preference, since each person’s body chemistry is different. Keep reading to learn about how this simple and effective deodorant may benefit you. ## How to use crystal deodorant Crystal deodorant is available as a stone, roll-on, or spray. Sometimes you can find it as a gel or powder. If you use a stone, it may come on its own or attached to a plastic base. The best time to apply the deodorant is right after you shower or bathe, when your underarms are freshly cleaned and still slightly damp. You can apply it to other body parts as well, but you may wish to have a separate stone for this. Run the stone under water and then apply it to clean underarms. Make sure you don’t use too much water. If you’re using a stone that’s attached to a plastic applicator, make sure the water doesn’t go into the base. You can store the stone upside down after use to prevent this from happening. You can rub it up and down or use a circular motion. Continue adding water to the stone and applying it until you feel you’ve covered your entire underarm. It should feel smooth as you’re applying it. Be careful if your stone is cracked or has any rough edges that might cut or irritate your underarms. Continue to rub until the underarm is dry. If you’re using a spray, you may want to have a towel wrapped around your body that can catch any excess liquid that might run down from your underarm. There may be a slight chalky residue left on your skin after application, so it’s a good idea to wait until the deodorant dries before getting dressed. Crystal deodorant may be effective for up to 24 hours. If you wish to apply the deodorant in between showers, you can clean your underarm using rubbing alcohol and a cotton ball before reapplying. The salt in crystal deodorant helps kill bacteria that cause underarm odor. While you may still sweat, the odor may be reduced or eliminated. ## Crystal deodorant benefits Part of the allure of crystal deodorant is that you’re able to avoid the chemicals found in conventional deodorant. Wearing deodorant and antiperspirant may inhibit the release of toxins from your body. Preventing your body from sweating naturally is thought to lead to clogged pores and a buildup of toxins. Common deodorants and antiperspirants may contain the following chemicals: - aluminum compounds - parabens - steareths - triclosan - propylene glycol - triethanolamine (TEA) - diethanolamine (DEA) - artificial colors Many of these chemicals are thought to be harmful to your health and may irritate sensitive skin. It’s important that you read the ingredient list for all deodorants, even if they’re labeled “natural.” Keep in mind that scented crystal deodorants could contain other ingredients. Carefully read the entire ingredient list. Stone crystal deodorant can last several months. However, it has the potential to develop an odor after some time. It will be less likely to develop an odor if your underarms are free of hair. If the smell is a problem, try using a crystal deodorant spray, since it won’t come into contact with your underarms. Prices for crystal deodorant vary but are comparable to conventional deodorant and sometimes cheaper, especially if you use a stone. The potential for increased body odor during this adjustment phase also exists. Usually your body will adjust after some time. Crystal deodorant may cause rashes, itchiness, or irritation, especially if your skin is broken or you’ve recently shaved or waxed. It can also cause an allergic reactionTrusted Source such as inflammation, dryness, or redness. Avoid use when your skin is sensitive and discontinue use if the crystal deodorant continually irritates your skin. ## Takeaway Crystal deodorant may be one natural option. It will come down to a matter of personal preference and how well it works and reacts with your body, lifestyle, and clothing. It may even work better for you during certain seasons. You may want to make dietary and lifestyle changes that can help you reduce body odor. If crystal deodorant doesn’t work for you but you still want to find a natural deodorant, you can check out other options.

**Advances in Synthetic Thermal-Insulating Outerwear for Extreme Alpine Environments**  

**Abstract**  
Recent developments in textile engineering have enabled the creation of high-performance outerwear optimized for extreme alpine conditions. This paper examines innovations in synthetic fabrics and breathable membrane technologies that aim to achieve a balance between thermal retention and moisture regulation. By integrating lightweight insulation systems with advanced vapor-permeable barriers, manufacturers have produced garments that address the dual challenges of sub-zero temperatures and high exertion rates during high-altitude climbs. Laboratory and field evaluations demonstrate that these materials not only maintain core body warmth but also mitigate condensation-related heat loss, offering significant improvements in safety and comfort for mountaineers.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Alpine environments present a unique thermal management challenge: climbers must contend with severe cold, high winds, and variable humidity, all while maintaining mobility and preventing moisture accumulation from perspiration or environmental exposure. Traditional outerwear relying solely on bulk insulation often compromises breathability, leading to internal condensation and reduced thermal efficiency [1]. Conversely, garments designed for maximum ventilation may fail to preserve adequate warmth in sub-zero conditions. Recent synthetic fabric technologies, coupled with breathable membranes, have sought to reconcile these competing needs, enabling climbers to sustain prolonged activity without succumbing to cold stress or overheating.

---

**2. Synthetic Insulation Materials**  
Synthetic insulation fibers, such as polyester microfibers and hollow-core filaments, have emerged as leading alternatives to natural down in alpine applications. Unlike down, these materials retain much of their loft and insulating capacity when wet, an essential property in snow-laden or high-humidity environments [2]. Innovations in fiber crimping and cross-sectional geometry have enhanced thermal efficiency per unit weight, allowing for thinner garment profiles without sacrificing warmth. Multi-denier blends combine fine fibers for heat retention with coarser fibers for structural resilience, yielding insulation layers that resist compression under load.

---

**3. Breathable Membrane Technologies**  
Breathable membranes—microporous and monolithic—are critical to moisture management in alpine outerwear. Microporous membranes, typically composed of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE), allow water vapor molecules to pass while blocking liquid water ingress [3]. Monolithic membranes, often polyurethane-based, rely on molecular diffusion for vapor transmission and can be engineered to adapt permeability based on temperature and humidity gradients. Hybrid constructions integrate both membrane types, optimizing vapor release during high activity and sealing against wind-driven precipitation during rest phases.

---

**4. Fabric–Membrane Integration Strategies**  
The performance of thermal-insulating outerwear depends on the synergy between insulation layers and membrane systems. Laminated composites bond insulation directly to membrane-backed shell fabrics, reducing bulk and preventing cold spots caused by shifting layers. Alternatively, free-hanging liners allow for greater mechanical separation, which can improve airflow during exertion but may increase assembly complexity. Seam-sealing techniques have evolved to maintain waterproof integrity without excessively restricting breathability, using narrow-tape applications and low-temperature adhesives to preserve fabric hand.

---

**5. Field Performance and Testing**  
Controlled chamber tests and high-altitude field trials reveal that garments employing advanced synthetic insulation and breathable membranes maintain stable microclimates within the clothing system. Core temperature retention remains within optimal ranges even during extended exposure to -20 °C ambient temperatures combined with high wind speeds. Moisture accumulation, measured via relative humidity sensors within the insulation layer, is significantly reduced compared to conventional non-breathable designs, lowering the risk of evaporative heat loss and frost formation inside the garment [4].

---

**6. Conclusion**  
The convergence of synthetic insulation engineering and breathable membrane innovation has transformed alpine outerwear, enabling climbers to operate effectively in extreme conditions with reduced risk of cold-related injury. Future research should focus on adaptive insulation systems capable of dynamically modulating thermal resistance in response to environmental and metabolic changes, as well as sustainable manufacturing practices that minimize ecological impact.

---

**Designing an Ornamental Perennial Garden: Color Palettes, Bloom Timing, and Visual Impact**  

When crafting an ornamental perennial garden, the interplay between color, seasonal rhythm, and structural form is the foundation of lasting beauty. Unlike annual displays, perennials return year after year, developing a sense of permanence and character that matures over time. Thoughtful design ensures that a garden remains engaging from early spring through late autumn, and even into winter when seed heads and foliage silhouettes provide texture against frost.  

### Establishing a Color Palette  

A cohesive color palette is the cornerstone of an ornamental scheme. Begin by deciding whether you prefer harmonious blends or bold contrasts. Harmonious palettes often use analogous colors—shades adjacent on the color wheel, such as purples, blues, and soft pinks—to create a calming atmosphere. Contrasting palettes, on the other hand, employ complementary colors, like yellow and violet or orange and blue, for dynamic visual tension.  

Layering tones can add depth. For example, pairing deep burgundy foliage of Heuchera with pale lavender blooms of Nepeta creates a sophisticated gradient. White-flowering perennials such as Gaura or Shasta daisies can act as visual “rest stops,” breaking up stronger colors and preventing the scheme from becoming overwhelming.  

### Timing the Bloom Sequence  

One of the joys of perennial gardening is orchestrating a succession of blooms. Early spring can be heralded by primroses, Pulmonaria, and creeping phlox, which provide splashes of color as the garden awakens. Late spring and early summer might feature peonies, irises, and foxgloves, offering height and drama.  

Mid-summer is the season for exuberance: coneflowers, daylilies, and bee balm dominate, while ornamental grasses begin to develop their seed heads. In late summer to autumn, asters, sedums, and Japanese anemones carry the garden into its final flourish, often accompanied by the warm hues of turning foliage.  

By mapping bloom times for each plant, you can ensure there is no “gap” in display. This requires balancing early, mid, and late season performers, with some plants offering extended flowering periods to bridge transitions.  

### Creating Visual Impact Through Structure and Repetition  

Color and timing are enhanced by the underlying structure of the planting. Tall, vertical accents such as delphiniums or hollyhocks create focal points, while mounded forms like catmint or hardy geraniums fill space with softness. Spiky textures from plants like Veronica or ornamental alliums contrast beautifully with rounded blooms, adding visual intrigue.  

Repetition is a powerful tool in ornamental design. Repeating a particular plant or color at intervals leads the eye through the garden, creating rhythm and unity. For example, clusters of purple coneflowers placed at regular points can tie together areas with different supporting plants.  

Pathways, seating areas, and water features can be integrated into the planting scheme to offer varied perspectives. A bench framed by tall grasses and late-blooming perennials invites visitors to linger and appreciate subtle seasonal changes.  

### Considering Foliage and Off-Season Interest  

While flowers often take center stage, foliage provides the backdrop and carries the garden’s beauty beyond the bloom period. Variegated leaves, silver foliage, and bold architectural forms add texture. Hostas, ferns, and ornamental grasses can be chosen for their ability to thrive in shade or sun, complementing flowering plants.  

Winter interest can be achieved through plants with persistent seed heads, striking bark, or evergreen leaves. The dark seed clusters of Rudbeckia, the feathery plumes of miscanthus, and the red stems of dogwood shrubs all contribute to a garden’s year-round appeal.  

### Bringing It All Together  

An ornamental perennial garden is a living composition that evolves with each season. By selecting plants for their color harmony, staggered bloom times, and contrasting structures, you create a space that remains vibrant and engaging over many years. The artistry lies in balancing immediate visual impact with long-term sustainability, ensuring that the garden not only delights in its first season but continues to mature gracefully.  

Ultimately, the most successful designs are those that reflect the gardener’s personal style while honoring the rhythms of nature. Whether you prefer a serene wash of blues and whites or a bold tapestry of reds and golds, the principles of color, timing, and structure will guide you toward a garden that tells its own story throughout the year.

**ABSTRACT** The Geothermal Electricity Technology Evaluation Model (GETEM) is an essential tool for the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Geothermal Technologies Office (GTO) to understand the performance and cost of technologies it is seeking to improve. This detailed model is used for supply curve analyses, assessing the current economic feasibility and levelized cost of energy (LCOE) of hydrothermal geothermal systems and enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), and evaluating the potential impact of advanced geothermal technologies. GETEM can be used to estimate the performance and costs of currently available U.S. geothermal power systems. It is also used to estimate the costs of technologies 5 to 20 years in the future, given the direction of potential research, development, and demonstration (RD&D) projects. The model is intended to help GTO determine which proposed RD&D programs and projects might offer the most efficient improvement when using taxpayer funding. The model requires annual updates as well as revisions to reflect the current state of the art. Drilling costs are a significant portion of total geothermal development costs. The current GETEM drilling cost inputs rely on drilling data from 2009 and require an updated analysis of more recent data to ensure they remain representative of current technologies. An updated, more accurate understanding of costs could help the geothermal industry secure project development financing and investment funding and better allow the oil and gas (O&G) industry (both operators and service companies) to weigh potential geothermal market participation and customization. This report details recent drilling improvements from the Utah Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy (FORGE) and the O&G sector, comparing drilling performance and costs with values in GETEM, particularly the baseline drilling cost curves. Although drilling performance at FORGE has improved significantly, we did not find associated cost decreases that would justify lowering the GETEM baseline cost curves at this time. **1. Introduction** Drilling costs can account for up to 50% of the capital cost of developing a representative 50- megawatt (MW) geothermal plant (Tester 2006). In addition, it is thought that drilling costs could exceed 75% of the total project cost of EGS developments (Petty et al. 2009). Indeed, drilling costs are a significant fraction of any geothermal development’s total cost and ensuring they are accurate is vital to the planning and development of geothermal projects. The most recent geothermal cost analysis was conducted in 2017 as part of the landmark U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) GeoVision study (GeoVision 2019). In “GeoVision Analysis Support Task Force Report: Reservoir Maintenance and Development,” Lowry et al. applied the lessons and data from numerous previous geothermal drilling studies (e.g., Tester et al. 2006; Polsky et al. 2008; Bush and Siega 2010; Finger and Blankenship 2010; Sanyal and Morrow 2012; Lukawski et al. 2014; Yost et al. 2015; DOE 2016; Lukawski et al. 2016) to create up-to-date geothermal cost curves using the Well Cost Simplified (WCS) model (Lowry et al. 2017). These studies relied on drilling data from oil and gas (O&G) wells through 2009 and geothermal wells through 2013. However, the drilling sector in both industries has continued to make efficiency and technology advancements throughout the past decade. This report examines drilling data from the American Petroleum Industry (API) Joint Association Survey (JAS) on 2019 drilling costs and data from Utah FORGE to compare with and potentially update the baseline drilling cost curves used in GETEM. **4. Conclusions** Ensuring that the cost curves used in GETEM accurately reflect the current geothermal industry is essential for GTO, industry stakeholders, and other decision makers in geothermal. Due to the sparsity of publicly available data, these cost curves were based on broad literature reviews of geothermal and O&G data prior to 2013 (Lowry et al. 2017). In this report, the GETEM cost curves have been revisited and compared with more recent O&G data and new geothermal drilling results from the Utah FORGE site. The key insights from these sources of well cost data are: Despite advancements in pre-Covid O&G drilling performance over the last 10 years, drilling costs have remained relatively constant. Results from the most recent Utah FORGE wells show significant increases in ROP in hard rock with the use of PDC bits and drilling efficiency measures. Well average ROPs are double the values used in the creation of the baseline GeoVision cost curves used in GETEM. Increasing the ROPs in the GeoVision WCS runs to match the FORGE ROPs decreases the cost curves by approximately 10%. However, FORGE well costs, even when adjusted to be more representative of development wells, align more accurately with the unrevised baseline cost curves. Overall, the last decade has seen relatively constant drilling costs in O&G but noted improvements in drilling performance in geothermal wells as industry stakeholder adopt new tools and techniques. However, these improvements have not yet translated to costs lower than the baseline curves. Total well costs are also dependent on site, rig costs, and many other factors besides ROP. To justify a baseline cost curve update, a larger sample of final well costs from FORGE and the geothermal industry must be examined and demonstrate total well costs below the current baseline curve. Accordingly, we do not recommend a decrease to the GETEM baseline cost curves at this time. Our analysis of well costs also shows the limited impact of ROP on total geothermal well costs. Though higher ROPs decrease drilling time and associated costs, it has no effect on other costs such as the time and material costs associated with casing and cementing. To further reduce geothermal costs, these costs must also be decreased. As more geothermal is deployed and recent improvements are embraced by industry, the GETEM curves should be reexamined.

**City’s Main Train Station Breathes Easier After Major Ventilation Overhaul**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

The city’s busiest rail hub has undergone a significant transformation this year, following the completion of a multimillion-dollar upgrade to its ventilation system. Officials say the improvements have already made a noticeable difference, particularly during the peak summer travel season, when heat and stagnant air have long been a concern for commuters.  

**A Long-Awaited Modernization**  

For decades, the main train station—an architectural landmark dating back to the early 20th century—has struggled to balance historical preservation with modern infrastructure needs. The vaulted ceilings and enclosed platforms, while aesthetically striking, often trapped warm air and limited natural airflow. In recent summers, passengers reported stifling conditions during rush hour, prompting calls for intervention.  

The new ventilation project, initiated in 2021, was designed to address these issues without compromising the building’s historic character. Engineers installed a series of high-capacity air handling units, strategically positioned to maximize circulation across concourses and platform areas. These units are equipped with variable-speed fans that adjust output in real time, responding to changes in passenger density and outside temperature.  

**Technology Behind the Upgrade**  

According to the city’s transportation department, the system uses a combination of displacement ventilation and targeted extraction to move fresh air through the station. Cool air is introduced at floor level, pushing warmer air upward toward ceiling-level vents where it is expelled. This method not only maintains a more stable temperature but also reduces the feeling of stuffiness that had been a frequent complaint.  

Sensors placed throughout the station continuously monitor temperature, humidity, and air movement. Data from these sensors feed into a centralized control system, allowing operators to fine-tune performance. In addition, the system incorporates energy recovery technology, capturing waste heat in winter months to reduce overall energy consumption.  

**Impact on Passenger Comfort**  

Early feedback from commuters has been overwhelmingly positive. “Last summer, waiting for a train at 5 p.m. felt like standing in a sauna,” said local resident Maria Lopez. “Now it’s noticeably cooler, even when the station is packed.”  

Temperature readings taken during July and August show an average reduction of 4–6°C on platforms compared to pre-upgrade levels. The improved airflow has also lessened the concentration of heat pockets in congested areas, making it easier for passengers to move through the station without discomfort.  

**Operational Benefits**  

Station staff have reported that the new ventilation has eased strain on other building systems. Escalators and ticket machines, which previously experienced occasional shutdowns due to overheating, have operated more reliably since the upgrade. The enhanced airflow has also reduced condensation in certain areas, lowering maintenance needs for electrical equipment.  

Furthermore, by maintaining more consistent indoor conditions, the system supports better working environments for station employees, from ticket clerks to security personnel, who spend long hours on-site.  

**Balancing Heritage and Innovation**  

One of the most challenging aspects of the project was integrating modern ventilation equipment into a protected historic structure. Project engineers worked closely with heritage conservationists to ensure that ductwork, vents, and control panels were installed discreetly. In some cases, air intake grilles were custom-designed to mimic existing architectural details, blending seamlessly with the station’s stone and ironwork.  

“From the beginning, we were committed to preserving the station’s visual identity,” said project lead architect Daniel Cheng. “We wanted passengers to feel the difference in comfort, not to see obvious signs of the intervention.”  

**Looking Ahead**  

City officials view the ventilation upgrade as part of a broader commitment to modernizing public transport infrastructure. Plans are already in motion to apply similar improvements to other high-traffic stations in the network, with the goal of enhancing comfort and operational efficiency system-wide.  

Transportation Commissioner Aisha Rahman noted that while the immediate benefits are most apparent during summer, the new system will also improve conditions year-round. “Better airflow isn’t just about cooling,” she said. “It’s about creating a consistently pleasant environment for everyone who passes through our stations, regardless of the season.”  

**Public Reception and Future Monitoring**  

The transportation department has invited commuters to share their experiences via an online feedback portal. This data will help refine system settings and guide future upgrades. Independent assessments are scheduled for next year to measure the long-term impact on passenger comfort and infrastructure performance.  

For now, though, the consensus among travelers is clear: the main train station has never felt more welcoming. With its blend of historic charm and modern engineering, the station is set to remain a central, and now more comfortable, gateway to the city for years to come.

**Advances in Carbon Capture and Storage: New Pathways to Reduce Industrial Emissions**  

In the global effort to curb greenhouse gas emissions, carbon capture and storage (CCS) has emerged as a critical technology for mitigating the environmental impact of power generation and heavy industry. Recent developments in CCS systems are promising both in terms of efficiency and cost-effectiveness, with several projects demonstrating that large-scale deployment could be economically viable in the near future.  

Over the past decade, research teams and private companies have refined methods to sequester carbon dioxide from coal- and gas-fired power plants, cement kilns, steel mills, and other high-emission facilities. Traditional CCS involves capturing CO₂ from flue gases, compressing it, and injecting it into deep geological formations where it can be stored for centuries. While early systems were criticized for high energy demands and capital costs, innovations in sorbent materials, process integration, and monitoring technology are beginning to address these concerns.  

One of the most notable advances lies in the use of novel solid sorbents that can absorb CO₂ at lower temperatures and release it under mild conditions, reducing the energy penalty associated with capture. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), for example, offer high surface area and tunable chemistry, enabling selective CO₂ capture even in the presence of moisture—a common challenge in industrial exhaust streams. Pilot plants using MOF-based systems have reported capture efficiencies above 90% with significantly reduced regeneration energy compared to conventional amine-based solutions.  

In parallel, engineers are improving post-combustion capture processes by integrating them more tightly with plant operations. Some facilities now employ waste heat recovery to drive the capture cycle, cutting operational costs. Others are exploring oxy-fuel combustion, which produces a flue gas that is mostly CO₂ and water vapor, simplifying separation and compression.  

Storage solutions are also advancing. Geological sequestration in saline aquifers remains the most widely studied approach, with extensive mapping of suitable formations across North America, Europe, and Asia. Enhanced oil recovery (EOR) projects have long used CO₂ injection to boost production, and these operations are increasingly being repurposed for permanent storage once reservoirs are depleted. More novel is the concept of mineralization, where CO₂ reacts with certain rock types to form stable carbonates. This process occurs naturally over geological timescales, but researchers have found ways to accelerate it, as demonstrated in Iceland’s CarbFix project, which injects CO₂ dissolved in water into basalt formations, achieving solidification in under two years.  

Economic viability remains the central challenge for CCS. Capture costs have fallen in recent years, with some estimates placing them at $40–$60 per ton of CO₂ for large installations, down from over $100 a decade ago. Analysts point to economies of scale, improved plant integration, and better financing structures as key drivers of cost reduction. Government incentives, such as tax credits in the United States and carbon pricing in parts of Europe, are also making CCS more attractive to private investors. The U.S. 45Q tax credit, for instance, offers up to $50 per ton of CO₂ permanently stored, which can offset a substantial portion of operating expenses.  

Critics caution that CCS should not be seen as a silver bullet, noting that capture technologies do not address other environmental impacts of fossil fuel extraction and combustion. Nevertheless, proponents argue that for industries where emissions are difficult to eliminate—such as cement and steel—CCS may be the only practical path to deep decarbonization in the short to medium term.  

Several large-scale demonstration projects are currently underway. The Petra Nova facility in Texas, although temporarily idled due to low oil prices, showcased the feasibility of retrofitting existing plants. In Canada, the Boundary Dam project continues to operate, capturing around one million tons of CO₂ annually. Meanwhile, in Norway, the Longship project aims to establish a full CCS value chain, from capture at industrial sites to offshore storage in the North Sea, potentially serving as a model for other nations.  

With global emissions continuing to rise, the urgency for scalable solutions is evident. The convergence of improved capture materials, integrated plant designs, and supportive policy frameworks suggests that CCS could play a significant role in meeting climate targets. As costs fall and operational experience grows, the technology may transition from niche applications to a mainstream tool for managing industrial carbon output.  

If these advances maintain momentum, CCS could become a cornerstone in the portfolio of strategies needed to achieve net-zero emissions, complementing renewable energy expansion, efficiency improvements, and systemic changes in production and consumption. The coming decade will be a crucial test of whether the promise of carbon capture can be fully realized.
