Mulch becomes more economical when 1) herbicides cannot be used due to crop safety issues and hand weeding becomes the only recourse; 2) longer-term plants are being grown (one or more years in production), so there is more time to recoup the cost of mulch, and more herbicide applications can be eliminated; and 3) herbicide applications are often missed due to labor shortages or inclement weather resulting in weed control failures. ## Drawbacks of Mulching Organic mulch materials may come with potential drawbacks, such as their rapid degradation and requiring reapplication for longer-term nursery crops. This can lead to higher material costs and increased labor demands during the mulching process. Placing mulch against the trunks of container-grown plants may pose another concern, as it could elevate the risk of pest pressure, particularly pathogens, if irrigation is not managed properly. Applying mulch at a depth of 4 inches or more can negatively impact plant growth due to reduced soil aeration and slower soil warming (Greenly and Rakow 1995). Additionally, there's a disadvantage associated with the potential loss of material, whether through container blow-over or the susceptibility of lighter materials like rice hulls or sawdust to be carried away by strong winds or heavy rain. When mulch is lost due to wind or pot blow-over, it must be reapplied, which is much more costly than reapplying a preemergence herbicide.

# exBEERiment \| Brewing With Fruit: Sweet vs. Bitter Orange Peel In A Belgian Witbier #### _Author: Steve Thanos_ * * * While beer is often described as a concoction made with water, malt, hops, and yeast, many brewers rely on a bevy of adjuncts to create unique flavors, in fact some historical styles call for such additions. Witbier is one example of a beer that’s made with adjuncts, namely coriander and orange peel, the latter comes in two main varieties– sweet and bitter. According to numerous online references, sweet orange peel tends to impart beer with a more pronounced orange character while bitter orange peel contributes a more general citrusy character and slight bitterness. Typically, brewers of Witbier stick to using bitter orange peel, though there’s no hard and fast rule about this, and many brewers have reported satisfactory results using sweet orange peel. Admittedly, I don’t brew or drink much Witbier, but I’ve tried examples made with both sweet and bitter orange peel in the past. While both types of orange peel seemed to contribute the citrus character expected for this style, I’ve never compared beers made with either side-by-side and designed an xBmt to see just how different they are for myself. ## \| PURPOSE \| To evaluate the differences between a Witbier made with sweet orange peel and one made with the same amount of bitter orange peel. ## \| METHODS \| For this xBmt, I went with my house Witbier recipe, which I felt was simple enough to allow any differences caused by the type of orange peel used to shine through. ### _Prevalence Of Ego_ ### Recipe Details | Batch Size | Boil Time | IBU | SRM | Est. OG | Est. FG | ABV | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 5.5 gal | 60 min | 13.3 | 3.6 SRM | 1.052 | 1.007 | 5.91 % | | | **Actuals** | 1.052 | 1.007 | 5.91 % | ### Fermentables | Name | Amount | % | | --- | --- | --- | | Pale Red Wheat | 4 lbs | 44.44 | | Pilsner Malt | 4 lbs | 44.44 | | Oats, Flaked | 1 lbs | 11.11 | ### Hops | Name | Amount | Time | Use | Form | Alpha % | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Magnum | 10 g | 60 min | Boil | Pellet | 12 | ### Miscs | Name | Amount | Time | Use | Type | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Coriander Seed | 28 g | 10 min | Boil | Spice | | Orange Peel, Bitter/Sweet | 43 g | 10 min | Boil | Flavor | ### Yeast | Name | Lab | Attenuation | Temperature | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Whiteout (B44) | Imperial Yeast | 76% | 32°F - 32°F | ### Notes | | | --- | | Water Profile: Ca 40 \| Mg 13 \| Na 9 \| SO4 10 \| Cl 14 | ### Download | | | --- | | Download this recipe's BeerXML file | [](https://www.johnihaas.com/sabro/?utm_campaign=Haas&utm_medium=Display&utm_source=https://brulosophy.com/&utm_content=Sabro) After collecting 2 sets of water and lighting the flame to get them heating up, I weighed out and milled the grains. [](https://brulosophy.com/2015/09/10/6-tips-for-dealing-with-efficiency-problems/) Once the water for each batch was adequately heated, I incorporated the grains then checked to make sure both were at the same target mash temperature. [](https://brulosophy.com/2015/01/28/when-temperature-matters-most-reviewing-the-thermapen/) While the mashes were resting, I prepared the kettle hop additions. [](http://yakimavalleyhops.com/) Once each 60 minute mash was complete, I removed the grains then boiled the worts, adding the different types of orange peel along with coriander with 10 minutes left. [](https://brulosophy.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/04_sweetvsbitterorangepeelbelgianwitbier_sweetPEELbitter.jpg) At the end of the 60 minute boil, I quickly chilled the worts with my Hydra IC. [](https://brulosophy.com/2014/09/23/the-hydra-immersion-chiller-by-jaded-brewing-a-review/) Refractometer readings showed both worts achieved the same target OG [](https://brulosophy.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/06_sweetvsbitterorangepeelbelgianwitbier_sweetOG1052bitter.jpg) 1.052 OG The filled fermenters were placed in my chamber and left to finish chilling to my desired fermentation temperature of 68°F/20°C for a few hours before I pitched a pouch of Imperial Yeast B44 Whiteout into each. [](https://shop.greatfermentations.com/product/b44-whiteout-imperial-yeast/beer-yeast?a_brulosophy) With signs of fermentation activity absent after 3 weeks, I took hydrometer measurements showing the beers had reached the same target FG. [](https://www.morebeer.com/products/final-gravity-hydrometer.html?a_aid=brulosophy) 1.007 FG I then transferred the beers into CO2 purged kegs and placed them in my keezer where they were left to condition for a couple weeks before they were ready to serve. [](https://brulosophy.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/09_sweetvsbitterorangepeelbelgianwitbier_sweetGLASSESbitter.jpg) Left: sweet orange peel \| Right: bitter orange peel ## \| RESULTS \| Thanks to my homebrew club, Plainfield Ale and Lager Enthusists for allowing me to collect data during our monthly meeting! A total of 20 people of varying levels of experience participated in this xBmt. Each participant was served 1 sample of the beer made with sweet orange peel and 2 samples of the beer made with bitter orange peel in different colored opaque cups then asked to identify the unique sample. While 11 tasters (p<0.05) would have had to accurately identify the unique sample in order to reach statistical significance, only 10 did (p=0.09), indicating participants in this xBmt were unable to reliably distinguish a Witbier made with sweet orange peel from one made with the same amount of bitter orange peel. **_My Impressions:_** Out of the 5 semi-blind triangle tests I attempted, I correctly identified the odd-beer-out 3 times, and those were admittedly guesses. Likely as a function of bias, I initially perceived the beer made with sweet orange peel as having a subtle sweetness in the finish compared to the one made with bitter orange peel, but that basically faded when I was blind to what I was drinking. [](https://www.johnihaas.com/lupomax/) ## \| DISCUSSION \| In addition to the 4 standard ingredients used to make beer, brewers have seemingly endless options for adjuncts that contribute fun and unique characteristics. One such ingredient is orange peel, an arguably necessary addition in Witbier that’s available in both sweet and bitter varieties. Despite coming from different orange varieties, some view sweet and bitter peel as interchangeable, as the amount used in a standard batch of beer is quite small. The fact tasters in this xBmt were unable to reliably distinguish a Witbier made with sweet orange peel from one made with bitter orange peel indicates the difference imparted by each was small enough as to be difficult to perceive. Coming from the C. sinensis orange variety, sweet orange peel is said to contribute a notably more “orangey” flavor that’s widely recognizable, as these types of oranges are commonly consumed. Bitter orange peel comes from the C. aurantium orange variety and is known to lend a more general citrus character with some bitterness. It’s possible the stronger fermentation and coriander flavors in this Witbier covered up some of the nuanced characteristics imparted by either type of orange peel, or perhaps the amount used, as typical as it is, simply wasn’t enough to accentuate the differences. I’ve been curious about the differences between sweet and bitter orange peel for a while and was a bit surprised with how similar I perceived these beers to be, as I admittedly expected these beer to be easily distinguishable. While I don’t brew Witbier that often, when I do, I’ll likely stick to my typical approach of using the fresh zest of a sweet orange, as it’s easy and contributes a nice orange character. _If you have any thoughts about this xBmt, please do not hesitate to share in the comments section below!_

**Keeping Pests at Bay: Harnessing the Power of Citrus Peels Indoors**  

If you’ve ever peeled an orange or sliced a fresh lemon, you’ve released a burst of bright fragrance into the air. That invigorating aroma isn’t just pleasant to humans—it’s also a natural deterrent to certain household pests. Citrus peels contain essential oils and acidic compounds that can make indoor spaces less inviting to ants, moths, and other small intruders. By learning how to work with these natural materials, you can create simple, effective repellents without resorting to synthetic chemicals.  

### Why Citrus Works  

Orange and lemon peels are rich in limonene, a compound that gives them their characteristic scent. Limonene has been studied for its insect-repelling properties, particularly against ants and moths. For ants, the strong citrus aroma can disrupt the pheromone trails they follow, making it harder for them to navigate and find food sources. In the case of moths, the volatile oils act as a sensory irritant, discouraging them from lingering near stored clothing or pantry goods.  

The acidity of citrus peels also plays a role. When certain acids from the peel’s surface come into contact with insects, they can interfere with the pests’ outer protective layers or feeding behavior. While these effects are mild compared to commercial pesticides, they are often enough to reduce the presence of pests in a given area when used consistently.  

### DIY Citrus Peel Spray  

One of the easiest ways to put citrus peels to work is by making a simple spray. Start by collecting fresh orange or lemon peels—about one cup loosely packed. Chop them into small pieces and place them in a heatproof bowl. Pour over two cups of boiling water, cover, and let steep until the water cools. Strain out the peel pieces, reserving the infused liquid.  

For added potency, you can blend the cooled infusion with a teaspoon of white vinegar and a few drops of pure lemon essential oil. Pour into a clean spray bottle and use it to mist entry points, windowsills, and areas where you’ve noticed ant activity. The spray can also be lightly applied to shelves or cupboards where moths might be a problem, though it’s best to avoid direct contact with food.  

### Citrus Peel Sachets  

If you prefer a dry method, citrus peel sachets are a low-maintenance option. Spread fresh peels on a baking sheet and allow them to air-dry for several days, or place them in a low oven (around 200°F / 93°C) for one to two hours until crisp. Once dried, break them into small pieces and mix with other aromatic deterrents such as dried rosemary or lavender buds.  

Fill small breathable pouches—muslin bags or squares of cheesecloth tied with string—and tuck them into dresser drawers, closets, or linen cupboards. The combined fragrance of herbs and citrus will help keep moths away from fabrics and discourage ants from exploring storage areas. Replace sachets every few months to maintain their effectiveness.  

### Tips for Effective Use  

Citrus-based repellents work best as part of a broader pest prevention strategy. Keep indoor spaces clean and free of crumbs, store food in airtight containers, and regularly inspect potential entry points. While the aroma of citrus peels can deter pests, it is not a substitute for sealing gaps or repairing screens.  

It’s also worth noting that the freshness of the peels matters. Over time, the volatile oils dissipate and the scent weakens, reducing the repellent effect. For sprays, prepare only what you’ll use within a week or two. For sachets, refresh them periodically with new dried peels or a drop of citrus essential oil.  

### A Natural, Fragrant Solution  

Citrus peels offer a dual benefit: they bring a clean, uplifting scent to your home while helping to discourage certain unwanted guests. With a few simple steps, you can transform kitchen scraps into practical, eco-friendly tools for indoor pest management. Whether you opt for a zesty spray or subtly scented sachets, these homemade solutions can make your living space more pleasant and less hospitable to ants and moths—naturally.

Diesel oil and water 4. Diesel oil and coconut oil 5. Diesel oil, coconut oil and kerosene The temperature suitable for diesel boiling ranges from 60 to $1 5 0 \\mathrm { { } ^ { \\circ } C }$ . The duration of immersion and boiling varies from 10 to 30 minutes depending on the rattan species and their diameters. Usually the rattans are taken out from the boiling diesel when: there are no more air bubbles at the end of the immersed rattan, or air bubbles present at the end of the immersed rattan disappear upon exposure to the air, or the diesel solution above the rattan surface turns bluish in colour, or the rattans start to float in the diesel solution. Immediately after boiling, the canes are either cleaned with gunny rags and sawdust, washed with a spray of pressurized water containing cleaning detergents or brushed with a broom in a concrete tank containing cleaning detergents. **2.3. Drying of oil cured rattans** After the oil curing and cleaning process, the rattan poles are air-dried in an open ground. Different methods are: Leaning them vertically or horizontally on wooden frames (end-racking) Bundling them loosely tied at one end and placing them in a wigwam-like structure with their upper ends in contact with the ground. This position helps to accelerate the drying process. Small-diameter rattans of about $6 \\textrm { m }$ long are hung over a wooden stand or spread over wooden stackers placed on the ground. The drying period of the oil cured rattan ranges from 10 to 14 days depending on the species of rattan and the weather conditions. Scraped (with knives or a splitting machine to remove nodes) rattan dries faster than unscraped and larger size rattan. On the third to fifth day of drying, the canes are turned over so as to obtain uniform drying. They are considered dry and ready to be transferred to a shed when the stem surfaces turn yellowish in colour, when they are light in weight, and produce a high pitched sound when hit on a hard surface or object. The moisture content should be more or less below 20 percent. Studies on Calamus manan boiled in diesel oil showed that the average amount of moisture loss immediately after boiling is about 17 to $54 %$ from its green condition of 76 to $9 8 %$ moisture content (Abdul Latif, 1992). **Innovative Nanoparticle Membrane Filtration for Rainwater Treatment in Rural Communities**  

**Abstract**  
Access to clean and safe water remains a critical challenge for rural communities worldwide, particularly in regions reliant on harvested rainwater for domestic and agricultural purposes. This study examines the application of nanoparticle-enhanced membrane technologies to improve the quality of collected rainwater prior to storage. By integrating advanced filtration systems into existing rainwater harvesting infrastructure, rural communities can simultaneously address microbial contamination, chemical pollutants, and turbidity. Laboratory trials and pilot-scale implementations demonstrate that membranes embedded with functionalized nanoparticles offer superior contaminant removal efficiencies compared to conventional polymeric membranes, while maintaining feasible operational costs. The findings suggest that such systems can be adapted to low-resource settings, enhancing water security and public health outcomes.  

**1. Introduction**  
Rainwater harvesting has long been recognized as a viable method for supplementing water supplies in rural areas, particularly where centralized treatment facilities are absent [1]. However, harvested rainwater often contains a range of contaminants, including pathogens, heavy metals, and organic matter introduced from atmospheric deposition and roof catchment surfaces [2]. Without adequate treatment, these contaminants pose risks to human health and limit the usability of collected water for irrigation of sensitive crops.  

Recent advances in nanotechnology have yielded filtration membranes capable of removing contaminants at the molecular scale. Nanoparticle membranes, which incorporate materials such as silver, titanium dioxide, or graphene oxide into a polymer matrix, can provide multifunctional filtration—combining physical sieving with catalytic or antimicrobial activity [3]. These properties make them particularly suitable for decentralized water treatment systems in rural contexts, where maintenance simplicity and robustness are critical.  

**2. Materials and Methods**  
The filtration systems evaluated in this study consisted of hollow-fiber ultrafiltration membranes embedded with nanoparticles selected for their specific functional properties. Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were utilized for antimicrobial activity, while titanium dioxide (TiO₂) nanoparticles provided photocatalytic degradation of organic pollutants under sunlight exposure. Membranes were fabricated using phase inversion methods, ensuring uniform dispersion of nanoparticles within the polymer matrix.  

Pilot installations were deployed in three rural communities in subtropical regions, each equipped with rooftop rainwater catchment systems. Raw rainwater samples were collected during initial precipitation events, representing worst-case contamination scenarios due to accumulated debris and dust on rooftop surfaces. The filtration units were installed between the downpipe and the primary storage tank, allowing immediate treatment upon collection.  

Water quality analyses followed standard protocols, measuring turbidity, total coliform counts, E. coli presence, heavy metal concentrations (Pb, Zn, Cu), and chemical oxygen demand (COD). Comparative testing was performed against conventional ultrafiltration membranes without nanoparticle enhancements.  

**3. Results**  
Across all pilot sites, nanoparticle membranes demonstrated marked improvements in contaminant removal. Turbidity levels were reduced by >95%, compared to 78–85% for conventional membranes. Total coliform and E. coli counts were reduced to below detectable limits in treated samples, with no regrowth observed during 30 days of storage. Heavy metal removal efficiencies averaged 70–85%, depending on the initial concentration and specific metal species. COD reductions were notably higher in membranes containing TiO₂ nanoparticles, attributable to photocatalytic degradation under ambient sunlight conditions.  

Operational performance remained stable over a six-month evaluation period, with minimal fouling observed and cleaning requirements limited to monthly backwashing. The integration into existing rainwater harvesting systems required no specialized training for local operators beyond basic maintenance procedures.  

**4. Discussion**  
The results indicate that nanoparticle membranes provide a robust and effective means of improving harvested rainwater quality for rural communities. The multifunctionality of the embedded nanoparticles addresses both biological and chemical contamination in a single treatment step, reducing the need for multiple filtration stages. This is particularly advantageous in low-resource contexts, where cost and operational simplicity are paramount.  

While the capital cost of nanoparticle membranes remains higher than conventional polymeric membranes, the extended lifespan and reduced maintenance frequency offset initial expenditures over time. Furthermore, the potential for local fabrication using regionally available materials could further improve affordability and adoption rates.  

Future research should explore the long-term environmental impacts of nanoparticle release from membranes, as well as optimization of membrane composition for specific regional contaminant profiles. Additionally, coupling these filtration systems with renewable energy-powered pumping and storage solutions could extend their applicability in off-grid scenarios.  

**5. Conclusion**  
Nanoparticle membrane filtration represents a promising advancement in rural rainwater treatment, enabling communities to secure safer drinking and irrigation water directly at the point of collection. The technology’s adaptability, contaminant removal efficiency, and operational feasibility suggest that it can play a significant role in improving water security and public health in underserved regions.

**Report: Innovative Design Trends in Beverage Packaging for Enhanced Brand Recognition and Customer Engagement**  

---

**Executive Summary**  
The beverage industry has increasingly recognized packaging as a critical medium for brand differentiation and consumer interaction. This report examines current innovative design trends across three dominant packaging materials—glass, aluminium, and plastic—highlighting how aesthetic and functional features are being leveraged to strengthen brand identity and foster customer loyalty. Examples include embossed glass bottles that convey premium quality, metallic finishes on aluminium cans that create visual impact, and ergonomic plastic bottle shapes designed for convenience and tactile appeal.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Packaging serves as both a protective vessel and a marketing tool. In highly competitive beverage markets, visual and tactile cues influence purchase decisions as much as the product itself. Leading brands are investing in design innovation that not only meets functional requirements but also engages consumers emotionally. This report outlines notable developments in the design of glass, aluminium, and plastic beverage containers, focusing on the intersection of aesthetic enhancement and user experience.

---

**2. Embossed Glass Bottles**  
Glass packaging has long been associated with premium positioning in beverages such as wine, spirits, and craft sodas. Recent trends include the use of embossing—raised designs or lettering integrated into the glass surface.  
- **Brand Recognition**: Embossing allows logos, patterns, or signature typography to become a permanent part of the bottle, enhancing recognizability even after labels are removed or altered.  
- **Tactile Engagement**: The texture created by embossing offers a sensory dimension, encouraging consumers to physically interact with the product.  
- **Heritage and Authenticity**: Many heritage brands use embossed glass to signal tradition and craftsmanship, reinforcing brand narratives.  
Advances in moulding technology have expanded the range of intricate designs possible, enabling smaller producers to adopt this premium feature.

---

**3. Metallic Finishes on Aluminium Cans**  
Aluminium cans remain a popular choice for carbonated beverages and ready-to-drink products, with design innovations focusing on surface treatments.  
- **Visual Impact**: Metallic finishes—ranging from brushed textures to high-gloss coatings—enhance shelf appeal by catching light and drawing attention.  
- **Special Editions and Seasonal Campaigns**: Limited-run designs using metallic inks or holographic effects encourage collectors’ interest and repeat purchases.  
- **Integration with Printing Technologies**: Advances in digital can printing allow for precise application of metallic elements, gradients, and complex patterns without compromising recyclability.  
Such finishes are increasingly combined with tactile varnishes or embossed can surfaces to create multi-sensory engagement.

---

**4. Ergonomic Plastic Bottle Shapes**  
Plastic bottles, particularly PET (polyethylene terephthalate), offer flexibility in shaping, enabling brands to tailor ergonomics to specific consumer needs.  
- **Grip and Comfort**: Contoured designs improve handling, especially for on-the-go consumption, enhancing user satisfaction.  
- **Functional Innovation**: Integration of features such as built-in handles, twist contours for easier opening, and compatibility with sports caps expands utility.  
- **Brand Differentiation**: Unique silhouettes act as instant identifiers on crowded retail shelves, helping consumers locate preferred brands quickly.  
Advances in blow moulding allow complex curves and structural reinforcements without excessive material use, balancing visual appeal with durability.

---

**5. Cross-Material Design Strategies**  
Brands are increasingly employing cross-material design consistency, ensuring that core visual elements—such as logos, colour palettes, and signature shapes—translate across glass, aluminium, and plastic formats. This approach supports cohesive branding while allowing flexibility in product lines. For example, a craft brewery may maintain a distinctive embossed motif on its glass bottles while echoing the same pattern in metallic ink on its aluminium cans.

---

**6. Consumer Engagement and Digital Integration**  
Emerging trends link physical packaging design with digital engagement platforms. QR codes, augmented reality triggers, and NFC (near-field communication) chips embedded or printed onto bottles and cans create interactive experiences. These features can be seamlessly integrated into embossed patterns, metallic highlights, or ergonomic contours, ensuring that the digital layer complements rather than disrupts the aesthetic.

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Innovative packaging design is a key driver of brand recognition and customer engagement in the beverage sector. Embossed glass bottles convey authenticity and premium quality, metallic finishes on aluminium cans deliver striking visual appeal, and ergonomic plastic bottle shapes enhance functionality and comfort. By strategically leveraging the unique properties of each material, brands can create packaging that resonates with consumers and reinforces their identity in the marketplace.

---

**Horse-Drawn Carriages in 19th-Century European Cities**  

During the 19th century, horse-drawn carriages were not merely a mode of transport but a vital element of urban life in many European cities. Their cultural significance extended beyond practical utility, influencing patterns of tourism, shaping local economies, and contributing to the aesthetic identity of urban centers. This period saw a flourishing of carriage types, from utilitarian hansom cabs to ornate landaus, each reflecting both technological developments and social hierarchies.  

**Historical Context and Urban Integration**  
By the early 1800s, industrialization was transforming European cities, yet horses remained the primary means of urban conveyance. Carriage services were organized into regulated systems, with licensed drivers, established routes, and designated stands. In cities such as Paris, Vienna, and London, carriage traffic was integral to the daily rhythm, carrying residents to work, markets, theatres, and social gatherings. The presence of horse-drawn vehicles influenced city planning: broad boulevards, cobblestone paving, and covered arcades were designed with carriage accessibility in mind.  

**Cultural Significance in Tourism**  
Horse-drawn carriages played a central role in shaping the tourist experience in the 19th century. Visitors to European capitals often engaged carriage tours as a means to view architectural landmarks, parks, and cultural institutions. In Paris, for example, carriages offered scenic rides along the Champs-Élysées, while in Vienna, elaborate fiacres transported tourists to the Ringstraße and the Prater. These rides were not only functional but also ceremonial, allowing travelers to participate in the visual and social spectacle of the city. The carriage ride itself became a sought-after leisure activity, symbolizing refinement and cosmopolitan engagement.  

**Economic Impact**  
The carriage industry supported a wide network of trades and services. Beyond the drivers, there were stable owners, grooms, farriers, harness makers, and carriage builders. The demand for well-bred horses stimulated rural economies, as breeders supplied urban stables with animals suited for speed, endurance, and aesthetic appeal. In cities, carriage hire fees contributed significantly to municipal revenues, particularly in tourist-heavy districts. Seasonal variations in tourism directly affected carriage operations, with summer months often yielding the highest profits due to increased travel and public events.  

**Artistic and Social Representation**  
Carriages frequently appeared in 19th-century art, literature, and theatre, symbolizing elegance, modernity, or social status. Painters captured scenes of bustling carriage stands or elegant couples alighting from coaches at opera houses. Novelists used carriage rides as settings for pivotal plot developments, underscoring their role as both literal and figurative vehicles of movement through the city’s social fabric. Public spectacles, such as royal processions or civic parades, relied on richly decorated carriages to convey grandeur and legitimacy.  

**Technological Developments and Adaptations**  
Advancements in suspension systems, wheel design, and harnessing techniques improved passenger comfort and safety. Innovations such as the hansom cab’s low center of gravity allowed for greater maneuverability in crowded streets. Municipal authorities introduced regulations to manage carriage traffic, including speed limits and licensing requirements, in response to growing urban congestion. These measures reflected the carriage’s dual identity as both an economic asset and a potential source of disorder in densely populated areas.  

**Legacy and Decline**  
By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the advent of mechanized transport began to diminish the prominence of horse-drawn carriages. However, their cultural imprint remained strong. In many European cities, ceremonial and tourist-oriented carriage rides persisted, preserving the aesthetic connection to a bygone era. Today, surviving examples of 19th-century carriages are displayed in museums or employed in heritage tourism, offering tangible links to the traditions and urban landscapes of the period.  

In sum, horse-drawn carriages in 19th-century European cities were more than transport vehicles; they were integral to the cultural identity, economic vitality, and tourist appeal of metropolitan life. Their influence extended from the design of streets to the rhythms of daily activity, leaving a legacy that continues to inform historical understanding of urban development and leisure in the modern age.

It's no secret that Southerners love bacon. And that includes the grease, too. If you were raised in the South (or raised by someone who was), one of the first kitchen lessons you might have learned is to never pour bacon grease (or drippings) down the drain. Not only will hardened fats create a plumbing nightmare, bacon grease is a precious ingredient, almost as important as the bacon itself. Bacon grease adds savory, smoky depth to all kinds of recipes: skillet cornbread, succotash, buttermilk biscuits, pastas, and just about any type of cooked vegetable, to name a few. A container of bacon grease is a cook's secret weapon—and unlike pricey olive oils or fancy seasoning blends, it's something you already have on hand. Here's how to make sure you store this cooking treasure with all the care it deserves. Credit: Photo: Caitlin Bensel; Food Styling: Torie Cox ## How To Store Bacon Grease To safely store bacon grease, you must first get rid of any small bits of bacon that are left behind: - Place a coffee filter or cheesecloth over the mouth of a glass container, like a Mason jar, or a container made for bacon drippings. Press the filter down so that it fits snugly inside the mouth of the jar. - Slowly pour the warm (not hot!) bacon grease into the jar—don't rush this step. (It's easier to do this if you transfer the drippings from the skillet into a glass measuring cup.) The coffee filter will trap whatever is left behind in the grease, leaving it nice and clear. You can also use a fine mesh sieve if you don't have coffee filters or cheesecloth on hand. Removing the bacon bits will also help prevent the grease from going rancid. How To Cook Bacon In The Oven ## Where To Store Bacon Grease Although many of us grew up with relatives who stored their bacon grease in a jar or can set on the counter or on the back of the stovetop, food safety experts don't recommend storing it that way now. Instead, store bacon grease in the refrigerator (up to 3 months) or freezer (indefinitely). The refrigerator is best because the fat will stay soft enough to scoop, so you can have delicious solid drippings at the ready. If you plan to freeze your bacon grease, portion small amounts by letting the grease cool slightly—and, then, strain and pour into freezer-safe containers (like an ice cube tray). Pop it in the freezer and defrost it in the refrigerator overnight before using.

reclamation properties, and the ability to remove poisonous substances and

materials. This is because [ cannabis ](/wiki/Cannabis "Cannabis") processing
is done mechanically with minimal harmful effects on the environment. A part
of what makes hemp [ sustainable ](/wiki/Sustainability "Sustainability") is

](/wiki/Biodegradation "Biodegradation") , making hemp a popular choice in [

reinforce structures by embossing threads and cannabis shavers. Hemp has been
involved more recently in the building industry, producing building
construction materials including [ insulation ](/wiki/Thermal_insulation
"Thermal insulation") , [ hempcrete ](/wiki/Hempcrete "Hempcrete") , and
varnishes.  [39]  [40]  [41]  [42]  [43]  [44]

absorb large amounts of [ CO  2  ](/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") ,
providing air quality, thermal balance, creating a positive environmental
impact.  [40]

Hemp's properties allow mold resistance, and its porous materiality makes the
building materials made of it breathable. In addition hemp possesses the
ability to absorb and release moisture without deteriorating. Hemp can be non-
flammable if mixed with [ lime ](/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") and could be
applied on numerous aspects of the building (wall, roofs, etc.) due to its
lightweight properties.  [38]  [40]

### Tips for Extending Battery Lifespan #### Automatic battery health management. To reduce battery aging, built-in software and hardware systems are included to manage charging patterns and battery temperature. - Optimized Battery Charging and Optimized Charge Limit adapt to your daily usage and preserve your battery lifespan over time. Optimized Battery Charging is available on all platforms as of iOS 13, watchOS 7, and macOS Big Sur. Based on your daily charging routine, it may automatically defer charging to 100% until shortly before you need to use the battery. Apple Watch Ultra can further reduce time spent at high states of charge by learning when to charge to an Optimized Charge Limit and when to allow for a full charge. - Charging may pause temporarily while in extreme temperature conditions, and will resume once the battery’s temperature returns to its normal operating range. Starting in iOS 16, you may see a notification appear on the lock screen when charging has paused for this reason. Starting in iOS 16 and watchOS 9, paused charging information is also available in Settings > Battery. #### Avoid extreme ambient temperatures. Your device is designed to perform well in a wide range of ambient temperatures, with 62° to 72° F (16° to 22° C) as the ideal comfort zone. It’s especially important to avoid exposing your device to ambient temperatures higher than 95° F (35° C), which can permanently damage battery capacity. That is, your battery won’t power your device as long on a given charge. Charging the device in high ambient temperatures can damage it further. Software may limit charging above 80% when the recommended battery temperatures are exceeded. Even storing a battery in a hot environment can damage it irreversibly. When using your device in a very cold environment, you may notice a decrease in battery life, but this condition is temporary. Once the battery’s temperature returns to its normal operating range, its performance will return to normal as well. ##### iPhone, iPad, iPod, and Apple Watch Comfort Zone 32° F 95° F Too ColdRoom TemperatureToo Hot iPhone, iPad, iPod, and Apple Watch work best at 32° to 95° F (0° to 35° C) ambient temperatures. Storage temperature: -4° to 113° F (-20° to 45° C). ##### MacBook Comfort Zone 50° F 95° F Too ColdRoom TemperatureToo Hot MacBook works best at 50° to 95° F (10° to 35° C) ambient temperatures. Storage temperature: -4° to 113° F (-20° to 45° C). #### Remove certain cases during charging. Charging your device when it’s inside certain styles of cases may generate excess heat, which can affect battery capacity. If you notice that your device gets hot when you charge it, take it out of its case first. #### Store it half-charged when you store it long term. If you want to store your device long term, two key factors will affect the overall health of your battery: the environmental temperature and the percentage of charge on the battery when it’s powered down for storage. Therefore, we recommend the following: - Do not fully charge or fully discharge your device’s battery — charge it to around 50%. If you store a device when its battery is fully discharged, the battery could fall into a deep discharge state, which renders it incapable of holding a charge. Conversely, if you store it fully charged for an extended period of time, the battery may lose some capacity, leading to shorter battery life. - Power down the device to avoid additional battery use. - Place your device in a cool, moisture-free environment that’s less than 90° F (32° C). - If you plan to store your device for longer than six months, charge it to 50% every six months. Depending on how long you store your device, it may be in a low-battery state when you remove it from long-term storage. After it’s removed from storage, it may require 20 minutes of charging with the original adapter before you can use it.

**Architectural Evolution of Beverage Packaging Design: Branding, Aesthetics, and Consumer Psychology**  

---

**Abstract**  
Beverage packaging has undergone significant transformations over the past century, shaped by technological advances, shifts in consumer preferences, and evolving branding strategies. This paper examines the architectural evolution of beverage container design, with particular attention to the interplay between material choice, aesthetic form, and psychological appeal. Drawing upon historical case studies and contemporary market analyses, it argues that packaging architecture functions not only as a protective vessel but also as a communicative medium that reinforces brand identity and influences consumer behavior.  

---

**Introduction**  
The design of beverage packaging represents a convergence of engineering, marketing, and cultural symbolism. While functional considerations such as durability, portability, and shelf life are essential, they are inextricably linked to aesthetic and psychological factors that determine consumer engagement. Over time, the architectural form of beverage containers—whether cylindrical aluminium cans, contoured glass bottles, or ergonomic plastic bottles—has been shaped by both material constraints and brand narratives. Understanding this evolution requires examining how visual and tactile design elements are deployed to create perceived value and reinforce brand loyalty.  

---

**Historical Trajectory of Beverage Packaging Architecture**  
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, glass dominated the beverage industry, valued for its inertness and capacity to preserve flavor integrity [1]. The architectural design of glass bottles often included embossed logos and distinctive shapes, such as the iconic contour bottle introduced by Coca-Cola in 1915, which served as both a functional grip aid and a brand signature [2]. This period established a precedent for packaging as a brand differentiator rather than merely a storage solution.  

The mid-20th century saw the widespread adoption of aluminium cans, facilitated by advances in metal-forming technology and sealing mechanisms. The sleek cylindrical form offered efficient stacking, space optimization in transport, and a broad printable surface for vibrant brand graphics [3]. Aluminium’s malleability enabled subtle variations in rim and base design, enhancing both structural integrity and visual appeal.  

Plastic bottles emerged prominently in the latter half of the 20th century, driven by consumer demand for lightweight, resealable containers. The architectural flexibility of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) allowed for complex ergonomic shapes, integrated grips, and distinctive neck profiles that reflected brand ethos [4]. The transparency of PET also supported visual engagement with the product itself, reinforcing perceptions of freshness and purity.  

---

**Branding and Aesthetic Strategies**  
Material selection directly informs the aesthetic language of packaging architecture. Glass conveys premium quality and tradition, often paired with minimalist or artisanal visual design to appeal to heritage-conscious consumers. Aluminium, with its metallic sheen and smooth surface, aligns with modern, dynamic branding, frequently used in energy drinks and craft beer markets. Plastic’s design versatility enables bold contouring and vibrant labeling, targeting convenience-oriented demographics.  

Color, typography, and surface finish interact with container shape to create a cohesive brand experience. For example, matte finishes on aluminium cans evoke sophistication, while high-gloss PET bottles emphasize vitality and freshness. The tactile experience—weight, grip, and temperature perception—also plays a critical role in consumer psychology, shaping repeat purchase behavior [5].  

---

**Consumer Psychology and Material Perception**  
Consumer responses to packaging architecture are mediated by cultural associations and sensory cues. Studies indicate that heavier packaging is often perceived as higher quality, even when the product inside is identical [6]. Conversely, ergonomic lightness can be associated with convenience and portability, resonating with active lifestyle branding. Transparency in packaging, whether through clear glass or PET, fosters trust by allowing visual inspection of the contents.  

Material tactility further influences brand perception: the smooth coolness of glass suggests refinement, the crisp opening sound of aluminium cans signals freshness, and the flexible resilience of plastic conveys adaptability. These sensory dimensions are strategically leveraged in marketing campaigns to reinforce product positioning.  

---

**Conclusion**  
The architectural evolution of beverage packaging reflects a dynamic interplay between material science, aesthetic innovation, and consumer psychology. From the ornate glass bottles of the early 20th century to the ergonomic PET designs of today, each shift in form and material has served both functional and communicative purposes. Packaging architecture remains a critical vector for brand differentiation, with design choices continuing to shape consumer perceptions and market success. Future developments will likely integrate sustainable materials with advanced design strategies, further aligning visual and tactile appeal with environmental and branding imperatives.  

---

[2] Allen, R. (2015). *Iconic Packaging Design: The Coca-Cola Contour Bottle*. Design Studies Quarterly, 28(1), 14–27.  
[3] Peters, M. & Wong, L. (2011). *Aluminium Can Innovation and Market Impact*. Materials & Marketing Review, 19(4), 102–118.  
[4] Johnson, K. (2019). *Plastic Bottle Design Evolution*. International Journal of Consumer Packaging, 33(2), 71–86.  
[5] Lee, A. (2017). *Tactile Branding: The Role of Touch in Consumer Packaging*. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 23(5), 321–339.

# ABSTRACT The particle size distribution of cigarette smoke is an important factor in predicting the deposition fraction of the inhaled particles in various regions of the respiratory tract. Mainstream cigarette smoke is a direct concern for smokers, while the exhaled and side stream smoke contribute to passive (second hand) smoking. The particle size distribution of tobacco smoke for mainstream and exhaled smoke has been studied in this work. This study investigates how smoking behavior, including puff volume and number of puffs, affect the particle size distribution of mainstream cigarette smoke. Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer (SMPS) was used to measure the particle size distribution of mainstream and exhaled cigarette smoke. The values of count median diameter (CMD) mobility size for the first four consecutive puffs were found to be 193 nm, $1 9 8 \\mathrm { n m }$ , $1 9 4 \\mathrm { n m }$ and $1 8 6 \\mathrm { n m }$ . As the volume of a puff increases from $3 5 ~ \\mathrm { m L }$ to $8 5 ~ \\mathrm { m L }$ , the CMD shifted slightly towards the higher particle size ranges, because of increased probability of coagulation and other combination processes. For the exhaled cigarette smoke, the growth factor was found to be $1 . 5 \\pm 0 . 3$ with respect to mainstream cigarette smoke. The experimental results of particle size distributions were used in a Multiple Path Particle Dosimetry (MPPD) model to predict deposition patterns in the human respiratory tract. The MPPD model results show the deposition fractions for mainstream cigarette smoke were 0.163, 0.152 and 0.298 for the head, trachea and bronchi (TB) and pulmonary region, and those for exhaled cigarette smoke were 0.273, 0.064 and 0.134 respectively. The total calculated deposition fraction for mainstream and exhaled cigarette smoke was found to be 0.613 and 0.471, respectively. Keywords: Particle size distribution; Mainstream cigarette smoke; Exhaled cigarette smoke; SMPS; Deterministic dosimetry model; Respiratory tract deposition. # INTRODUCTION Tobacco smoke is a complex mixture of gaseous compounds and particulates. Current literature shows 4800 identified gaseous and particulate bound compounds in cigarette smoke (Baker, 1999; Perfetti and Rodgman, 2008). Airborne particulate matter (PM), and especially fine particles, has been associated with various adverse health effects. Environment tobacco smoke (ETS) is an important source of anthropogenic pollution in indoor environments. Cigrette smoke made of gaseous pollutants as carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide $( \\mathrm { S O } _ { 2 } )$ , nitric oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide $\\left( \\mathrm { NO } _ { 2 } \\right)$ , methane $\\mathrm { ( C H _ { 4 } ) }$ , non-methane hydrocarbon (NMHC), carbonyls and volatile organic compounds (VOCs); and particulate matter (PM) (Diapouli et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012). In assessing the effects of cigarette smoke on smokers and nonsmokers, the particle size distribution of the aerosol is an important factor in predicting the deposition fraction of the inhaled particles in various regions of the respiratory tract (Chang et al., 1985). During cigarette smoking there are two dominant pathways of smoke generation. The mainstream smoke which goes as a puff in smoker’s mouth through filter and side stream smoke which is emitted in air from the burning end of cigarette (not through filter). Deposition of mainstream cigarette smoke (MCS) in the respiratory tract is a key mechanism for exposure of smokers to smoke constituents and in understanding smoking-related disease (Feng et al., 2007; Moldoveanu and St. Charles, 2007). The particles in Environmental Tobacco Smoke (ETS) are derived from particles in fresh mainstream and side stream smoke. However they undergo mixing and dilution (i.e., dispersion), and follow different routes of exposure over varying time scales in a particular indoor setting. While undergoing dispersion, the median tobacco smoke particle size can shrink as particle mass evaporates or can grow as particles coagulate (Klepeis et al., 2003). The mainstream smoke is a direct concern of smoker, at the same time the exhaled and side stream smoke combined, known as Environmental Tobacco Smoke (ETS) is responsible for passive smoking. Smoking can be simulated as a two-step process. The first step involves puffing of the cigarette and drawing smoke into the mouth where it is held for a finite period of time, as the palate generally closes off the mouth from the rest of the airways during puffing. After this step the second step is inhalation of the smoke into the lungs. Therefore the puffing process can be decoupled from the inhalation process. Various mechanisms have been put forward to explain the deposition pattern of cigarette smoke in respiratory tract, including coagulation, hygroscopic growth, condensation and evaporation, changes in composition, or changes in inhalation behavior (McGrath et al., 2009). The disparity which exists between experimental and predicted data from deposition models has still not been fully addressed in the literature (ICRP, 1994). This may be due to incomplete incorporation of parameters in predictive models for cigarette smoke deposition in respiratory track. The particle concentration in tobacco smoke is generally very high $1 0 ^ { 1 2 }$ particles per cigarette). Also, the hygroscopic nature of the smoke droplets results in rapid changes in particle diameter via coagulation and condensation (McRae, 1990). The three main mechanisms that affect the behavior of cigarette smoke particles in the respiratory tract are gravitational sedimentation, inertial impaction and Brownian motion (diffusion). Sedimentation and impaction are ‘aerodynamic’ effects that are important above about $1 ~ \\mu \\mathrm { m }$ and increase with increasing size. Aerodynamic effects are negligible for very small particles and thermodynamic effects are negligible for large particles. The deposition of smoke particle depends on the size of particle which may vary due to the high relative humidity condition in the respiratory tract. Despite the small diameter of the smoke particles, smoke deposition efficiencies of $6 0 { - } 8 0 %$ in the lung have been reported (Baker and Dixon, 2006). In this study an attempt has been made (1) to quantify particle size distributions for mainstream as well as exhaled cigarette smoke; (2) to study the effect of puffing conditions on the particle size distribution of fresh mainstream cigarette smoke (MCS); and (3) to evaluate the deposition of number concentration fraction in various compartments of the human respiratory tract for both main stream and exhaled cigarette smoke.

But there are certain cases where it would be nice to be able to create a
siphon without any intervention, a self-priming or automatic siphon: the next
level of siphonry. And this project is an example of just that. This is a
demonstration of a bell siphon which I built out of an acrylic sheet and a
piece of clear pipe. A bell siphon has three basic parts: a reservoir, the
bell, and a riser. Here’s how it works: as water fills the reservoir, the
surface of the water is equally exposed to atmospheric pressure. Outside the
bell, it’s exposed to the atmosphere from open top of the reservoir, and
inside the bell it’s exposed to atmospheric pressure through the empty riser
tube. As the water rises, it eventually forms a seal over the riser tube
inside the bell, closing off the bell’s connection to the atmospheric
pressure. As the water falls through the riser pipe, it creates a vacuum
inside the bell, drawing more water from the reservoir up and out. Eventually
the water level in the reservoir drops below the bell, allowing air to enter
and breaking the siphon. As the remaining water drains from the riser, the
pressure inside the bell returns to atmospheric and the process starts over
again.

The Drainage System is therefore the most important component of a highway or rural road, even in locations with only occasional rainfall. # PART D - DRAINAGE The Routine Maintenance\* of the drainage system is essential to preserve the road structure and running surface. **Rural Households Embrace New Generation of Compact Wood Pellet Stoves**  

*By Staff Writer*  

In recent years, rural homeowners seeking reliable, low-maintenance heating solutions have seen a surge in options for compact wood pellet stoves. These units, designed for household-scale use, combine modern combustion engineering with simplified installation, making them an increasingly attractive alternative to traditional wood-burning appliances.  

**Advances in Combustion Technology**  
Manufacturers have focused on refining the combustion process to maximize efficiency and minimize emissions. Modern compact pellet stoves employ precisely metered fuel feeds and electronically controlled airflow systems, ensuring that pellets burn at optimal temperatures. This controlled environment promotes more complete combustion, reducing particulate matter and increasing heat output per unit of fuel. Many models now incorporate ceramic or stainless-steel combustion chambers, which retain heat longer and facilitate thorough burning of the pellets.  

An important innovation has been the use of secondary burn systems. These systems channel preheated air into the combustion chamber at specific points, igniting gases that would otherwise escape unburned. The result is both improved energy efficiency and a cleaner exhaust, aligning with stricter air quality regulations in many rural regions.  

**Energy Efficiency Ratings**  
Independent testing agencies have begun publishing standardized energy efficiency ratings for pellet stoves, giving consumers a clear benchmark for comparing models. Top-tier compact units currently achieve efficiencies of 80–90%, meaning that most of the energy stored in the pellets is converted into usable heat. This performance rivals, and in some cases surpasses, that of larger central heating systems.  

For rural households without access to natural gas or with unreliable electrical grids, these efficiency gains translate directly into reduced fuel costs and fewer deliveries or trips to purchase pellets. In areas where pellet production uses locally sourced biomass, the environmental footprint can be further minimized, and the economic benefits remain within the community.  

**Ease of Installation and Use**  
One of the driving factors behind the popularity of these stoves is their straightforward installation process. Many compact units are designed for plug-and-play operation, requiring only a standard household electrical outlet and a properly vented flue. This eliminates the need for extensive retrofitting or specialized construction.  

Lightweight designs—often under 150 pounds—mean that homeowners can place units in living rooms, kitchens, or other central spaces without structural reinforcement. Some models feature top or rear venting options, allowing flexibility to accommodate existing chimney layouts or wall vents.  

User-friendly digital controls have replaced the manual dampers and levers of older stoves. Modern interfaces allow operators to set desired room temperatures, schedule heating times, and monitor performance data. Several manufacturers have introduced smartphone-connected apps, enabling remote adjustments and alerts for pellet refills or maintenance needs.  

**Economic and Environmental Considerations**  
While initial purchase prices for high-efficiency compact pellet stoves can be higher than those for conventional wood stoves, the long-term savings in fuel and maintenance often offset the difference. Pellets, made from compressed sawdust and other wood byproducts, are relatively inexpensive and have consistent moisture content, which contributes to predictable burn rates and heat output.  

Environmentally, the appeal lies in the closed-loop nature of the fuel supply. Pellets typically originate from waste materials in lumber production, reducing landfill contributions and making use of resources that would otherwise be discarded. The improved combustion systems also mean fewer emissions of fine particulates, a concern for communities conscious of air quality.  

**Looking Ahead**  
Industry analysts predict continued growth in the compact pellet stove market, driven by both technological advancements and shifting consumer priorities. As rural households seek independence from large-scale energy infrastructure, efficient and manageable heating solutions will remain in demand.  

Research and development efforts are focusing on integrating even more automation into the combustion process, experimenting with hybrid systems that can switch between pellet fuel and other biomass sources. Additionally, advances in durable materials and modular designs may further simplify maintenance and extend the lifespan of these appliances.  

For rural homeowners, the new generation of compact wood pellet stoves offers a blend of efficiency, convenience, and environmental responsibility. With ongoing innovation and increasing availability, these stoves are poised to become a staple in household heating for years to come.

**The Art and Tradition of Specialty Teas: From Leaves to the Perfect Brew**  

Tea has been cherished for centuries as both a daily comfort and an artisanal indulgence, woven deeply into cultural traditions across the globe. From the misty mountains of China’s Fujian province to the lush gardens of Assam, the journey of tea reflects a rich tapestry of history, craftsmanship, and evolving tastes. In recent decades, the world of specialty teas has expanded beyond traditional loose leaves to include a wide range of bagged options, each offering unique advantages and flavor profiles.  

**A Brief History of Specialty Teas**  
The origins of tea trace back over 4,000 years to ancient China, where legend tells of Emperor Shen Nong discovering the beverage when leaves fell into boiling water. Over centuries, tea spread across Asia, taking root in Japan’s meditative chanoyu ceremony and India’s robust chai culture. European traders in the 17th century further popularized tea, leading to distinct traditions such as Britain’s afternoon tea and Russia’s samovar gatherings. Specialty teas—those produced with careful attention to cultivation, processing, and varietal selection—emerged as a way to preserve and celebrate the most refined expressions of the plant.  

**Varieties and Flavor Profiles**  
Specialty teas encompass a range of types, each defined by processing methods and terroir:  

- **White Tea**: Minimally processed, often with delicate floral and honey notes.  
- **Green Tea**: Steamed or pan-fired to retain vegetal freshness, ranging from grassy Japanese sencha to nutty Chinese dragonwell.  
- **Oolong Tea**: Partially oxidized, offering complex layers from floral to roasted, prized in Taiwanese and Fujian traditions.  
- **Black Tea**: Fully oxidized, yielding bold, malty flavors; Darjeeling’s muscatel character contrasts with the deep richness of Yunnan teas.  
- **Pu-erh Tea**: Fermented and aged, producing earthy, mellow tones.  

Flavor profiles are influenced not only by oxidation but by leaf grade, harvest season, and cultivation altitude. Connoisseurs often seek out single-origin batches to experience the nuances of climate and soil.  

**Loose Leaf Versus Bagged Options**  
Loose leaf tea remains the gold standard for many aficionados, allowing leaves to unfurl fully during brewing and release their full aromatic range. The visual beauty of whole leaves and buds adds to the ritualistic appeal. Bagged teas, however, have evolved far beyond mass-market blends. Premium tea companies now offer sachets made with biodegradable materials and filled with high-quality, often whole or large-cut leaves. These combine convenience with respectable flavor complexity, making specialty teas more accessible to busy drinkers.  

The choice between loose and bagged often comes down to preparation style and desired intensity. Loose leaf tea offers more control over leaf quantity, steeping time, and water temperature, while bagged options provide consistency and ease.  

**Brewing Techniques for Optimal Flavor**  
Brewing specialty tea is a delicate balance of water temperature, steeping time, and leaf-to-water ratio. For green teas, water just below boiling (around 75–85°C) preserves subtle notes and avoids bitterness. Black teas generally benefit from fully boiling water, while oolongs vary depending on oxidation level. White teas, being delicate, should be steeped at lower temperatures for longer periods.  

Many cultures have codified their brewing rituals:  
- **Japanese Tea Ceremony**: Emphasizes harmony, respect, and mindfulness, with precise movements and tools.  
- **Chinese Gongfu Cha**: Involves multiple short infusions using small teapots, highlighting the evolving flavor over successive steeps.  
- **British Afternoon Tea**: Often includes milk and sugar, complementing robust black teas.  

Attention to detail—such as pre-warming the teapot, using filtered water, and timing the steep—can elevate the experience from simple refreshment to a sensory journey.  

**Cultural Traditions and Modern Trends**  
Specialty tea remains a bridge between the old and new. In Morocco, green tea with mint is served as a gesture of hospitality. In Tibet, butter tea offers warmth and sustenance in high-altitude climates. Contemporary tea culture, particularly in urban centers, blends tradition with innovation: tea sommeliers, tasting flights, and fusion blends (such as matcha lattes or jasmine-infused oolongs) appeal to adventurous palates.  

Today, tea drinkers can explore ancient traditions while embracing sustainable sourcing and artisanal production. Whether selecting hand-rolled oolong for a meditative brew or a premium bagged Darjeeling for convenience, the world of specialty teas offers endless opportunities to savor history, craftsmanship, and flavor in every cup.  

By understanding the origins, varieties, and brewing techniques, one can appreciate tea not just as a beverage, but as a cultural artifact—one that continues to evolve while honoring centuries of tradition.

# 4\. Discussion C. papaya belongs to a small family Caricaceae. It is succulent plant growing in tropical countries and sub-tropical regions of the world. Allelochemicals are released by different parts of the plant and leaves are most active in this respect (Rehman et al., 2014). The plant is reported to possess organic acids, alkaloids, tannins and flavonoids which hamper growth of adjacent plants (Canini et al., 2007). C. papaya is known to influence the growth of plants in its vicinity by the release of the allelochemicals during the decomposition of its litter (Christobel et al., 2017). Allelopathic potential of $C$ . papaya leaves for pest management is reported earlier. Crude aqueous leaf extracts of $C$ . papaya on susceptibility of fourth instar larvae of Spodoptera litura showed a significant total percent mortality (Deshmukhe et al., 2009). Therefore, allelopathic effect of leaves of C. papaya was evaluated for its aqueous extract as well as dry powder against five test species i.e., T. aestivum, A. fatua, H. annuus, Z. mays and $R$ . dentatus. For each test species, screening plant material was applied on filter paper and soil separately in both aqueous extract and powdered form that variably reduced the germination and growth of test plants. In our experiments, C. papaya affected germination of all test species. Similar to our results, inhibition of seed germination was observed in Sinapis arvensis by Glaucium species (Ghorbanli et al., 2011), in sorghum, sesame, sunflower and corn by mungbean (Lertmongkol et al., 2011), in chive and soybean by ginger (Han et al., 2008). Reigosa et al. (1999) proposed that allelochemicals affect physiological functions during germination thus hindering the process. It was reported that, seed characteristics such as seed coat permeability and seed size influence effects of allelochemicals in seeds and interference of the allelochemical compounds vary accordingly (Marianne et al., 2000). Similar results were proposed by Gherardi and Valio (1976) and Chow and Lin (1991) in bioassays with lettuce seeds and by Reyes et al. (1980) with cucumber seeds. Chow and Lin (1991) used extracts of sarcotesta and seeds of papaya, which showed presence of germination and growth inhibitors in the sarcotesta, halting the germination of lettuce seeds, which had also observed earlier by Gherardi and Valio (1976). They state that such inhibitors are phenolic in nature. In our study, most significant inhibition effects were found on A. fatua as compared to other test species. Similar results were reported by Turk and Tawaha (2003) showing negative germination effects of aqueous extract of Brassica nigra on A. fatua. A. fatua was also found to be a susceptible species against $P .$ hysterophorus (Batish et al., 2002; Marwat et al., 2008; Anwar et al., 2019). These observations have indicated that this test plant species is susceptible to number of allelopathic plants (Anwar et al., 2017a, 2018c). Radicle and plumule length inhibition was obsered in test species. Kato-Noguchi (2011) also observed epicotyl and hypocotyl inhibition by the allelopathic extracts of different plants. Similar results were reported by Oudhi (2001), Anwar et al. (2018d) and Maharjan et al. (2007). Allelopathic assessment of $C$ . papaya leaves, in our study, indicated that radicle length was more affected than plumule length. These findings support root sensitivity to allelochemicals compared to shoot. Relative greater root sensitivity may be explained by the fact, that after the seed germination, roots are first to be in contact with toxic compounds (Qureshi et al., 2014). Similar results were proposed by Fujii and Aziz (2005) while examining allelopathic effect of fourteen different plant species extracts on growth of lettuce seeds. The inhibitory actions under influence of allelochemicals are possibly due to reduction in cell division and cell size (Einhellig, 1996). The aqueous extract of C. papaya leaves, however, showed non-significant effect on wheat seeds germination, radicle and plumule growth. Similar results were reported by Tanveer et al. (2007) and Anwar et al. (2017b), where E. helioscopia was found to be non-toxic against wheat growth. Researches have suggested that a specific dose of these chemicals may cause growth stimulation (Pelinganga and Mashela, 2012). Abu El-Soud (2001) demonstrated growth stimulation in pea crop by Acacia nilotica leaf residue. Christobel et al. (2017) stated that $C$ . papaya aqueous leaf extract can be applied for growth improvement of Phaseolus aureus. Stimulation is suggested usually due to presence of growth promoting substances along with inhibitory substances (Yamada et al., 2010; Anwar et al., 2018a, b). The results of the present work clearly indicate that $C$ . papaya is a candidate of consideration for weed management in wheat crop. It was reported elsewhere that C. The papaya leaf extract is source of phenolic substances, acknowledged as the basis of allopathic properties of the plant species (Golisz et al., 2007). Understanding the mechanisms may contribute to the use of plant compounds as natural herbicide, which will help to limit use of synthetic herbicides.

Bell Siphon for Aquaponics
Using a bell siphon for aquaponics has become a very popular option, especially with ebb and flow setups becoming more and more common. This is because siphon devices like these offer many benefits when it comes to aquaponics. One of the most obvious benefits is the improvement in oxygenation to the roots of the hydroponic plants. In bell siphon grow beds, the action of the water draining draws oxygen through the full length of the root aiding in plant growth and the overall health of the plants. This compliments the ebb and flow’s benefits associated with flooding the roots with hydration and nutrients and then removing the water so oxygen can reach the roots. Another benefit to both the bell siphon grow beds and the fish is the constant and consistent movement of the water. Regular water flow improves oxygen in the water and prevents water stagnation.

# You Never Knew You Could Use The Peel From This Juicy Citrus Fruit As A Fire Starter By Robyn HuntJuly 25, 2023 6:30 am EST !roasting marshmallows around fire pitAnchiy/Getty Images After you've eaten your daily dose of vitamin C, don't throw out those peels. Orange peels contain flammable oils, primarily limonene. This high concentration of limonene allows them to ignite easily and sustain a flame, making them an effective and natural fuel source. This flammability, combined with the pleasant citrus aroma, makes citrus peels an environmentally-friendly choice for starting fires. Don't be afraid to experiment with other citrus fruits like mandarins, lemons, limes, and grapefruits. Using citrus fruit peels as fire starters is considered to be a sustainable fuel source for a few different reasons. First, you're repurposing the discarded peels, which is keeping them from fermenting in a landfill and contributing to greenhouse gas emissions. Second, using these fragrant citrus skins as kindling reduces the carbon footprint associated with manufacturing and transporting commercial alternatives. And, unlike some commercial fire starters, citrus peels offer a clean burn without emitting harmful chemicals or toxins. The non-toxic ash can be safely composted or used as a natural soil amendment. ## How to use citrus peels as fire starters !Basket of dried orange peelsInstagram To use orange peels as fire starters, begin by allowing the peels to dry out completely. Choose peels that are chemical and pesticide free, wash them, and blot them with a towel to remove any excess moisture. Lay the peels in a single layer on a clean surface, like a baking sheet or wire rack, and allow them to air dry in a well-ventilated area for two to four days. Placing them in front of a window, on top of your refrigerator, or above your fireplace are good locations. Once thoroughly dried and brittle, store the orange peels in a sealed airtight container or a Ziplock bag until you're ready to use them. An alternative for using orange peels as fire starters is to make firelighters. For this project, you'll need citrus peels and some wax, like beeswax or even old candles. Cut your citrus in half and scoop out the pulp. Melt the wax on your stove top until it turns into a liquid state. Carefully pour the hot wax into each of the citrus peel bowls, making sure that the wax thoroughly coats the inside of the peel. Allow the wax to harden, and store your firelighters in a cool, dark place. ## A word of caution about fresh peels !Man demonstrating orange peel flammabilityBurak Sür/Getty Images While you might be tempted to just toss your fresh orange peels into your fireplace, it's best to reserve them for use outside. The natural oils present in these peels also give off excessive smoke. Using citrus peels in your wood-burning fireplace can lead to issues with smoke and creosote buildup, notes Northco Fire. Creosote is highly flammable, and if left unchecked, it can pose a significant fire hazard. Over time, the accumulation of creosote in the chimney can restrict proper airflow, and worsen any smoke-related issues your chimney might already be having. **Report: Coastal Mangrove Restoration in Southeast Asia – Impacts on Biodiversity and Carbon Sequestration**  

---

**Abstract**  
Mangrove ecosystems along Southeast Asia’s coasts play a critical role in maintaining biodiversity, supporting local livelihoods, and mitigating climate change through carbon storage. This report examines recent restoration projects in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand, assessing their ecological outcomes and socio-economic implications. Findings indicate that targeted rehabilitation of degraded mangrove areas can significantly enhance species richness, bolster sustainable fishing practices, and contribute to measurable carbon sequestration.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Mangroves are intertidal forests that provide vital ecosystem services, including shoreline stabilization, nursery habitats for marine species, and high-capacity carbon sinks. Over the past decades, Southeast Asia has experienced large-scale mangrove loss due to aquaculture expansion, coastal development, and pollution. In response, regional governments and non-governmental organizations have initiated restoration projects aimed at reversing degradation trends. Such efforts align with broader climate change mitigation strategies and support the livelihoods of coastal communities dependent on fisheries and forest products.  

---

**2. Methods of Restoration**  
Restoration approaches vary by site but generally include:  

- **Reforestation with native species**: Planting Rhizophora spp., Avicennia spp., and Sonneratia spp. to re-establish natural forest composition.  
- **Hydrological rehabilitation**: Reconnecting tidal flows to areas cut off by dikes or embankments, allowing natural sediment deposition and seed dispersal.  
- **Community-based stewardship**: Empowering local fishers and residents to monitor mangrove health, enforce conservation regulations, and manage sustainable harvesting.  

Baseline biodiversity surveys and carbon stock measurements are conducted pre-restoration, with follow-up monitoring at regular intervals to evaluate project success.  

---

**3. Biodiversity Outcomes**  
Restored mangrove areas have shown marked increases in both terrestrial and aquatic species diversity. Key findings include:  

- **Fish populations**: Juvenile abundance of commercially important species such as snapper, grouper, and milkfish increased by 30–50% within three years of reforestation.  
- **Avifauna**: Migratory and resident bird species, including herons and kingfishers, returned to rehabilitated zones, indicating improved habitat quality.  
- **Invertebrates**: Crustacean diversity, particularly mud crabs and shrimp, rose in restored sites, supporting artisanal fisheries.  

The recovery of these populations contributes to ecosystem resilience, enhancing food security and income for local communities.  

---

**4. Carbon Sequestration Potential**  
Mangroves are recognized for their exceptional capacity to store carbon in biomass and sediments. Measurements from restored sites in North Sumatra and southern Thailand indicate:  

- **Aboveground biomass**: Average carbon storage of 100–150 tonnes C/ha within a decade of planting.  
- **Soil carbon**: Sediment cores reveal sequestration rates of 1.5–2.0 tonnes C/ha/year, significantly higher than many terrestrial forests.  

These figures underscore the role of mangrove restoration in meeting national greenhouse gas reduction targets under the Paris Agreement.  

---

**5. Socio-economic Impacts**  
Beyond ecological gains, restoration projects have had tangible socio-economic benefits:  

- **Sustainable fishing practices**: Enhanced fish stocks reduce pressure on overexploited offshore resources, allowing for more sustainable yields.  
- **Alternative livelihoods**: Communities engage in eco-tourism, mangrove honey production, and craft-making from non-timber forest products.  
- **Capacity building**: Training in nursery management, monitoring techniques, and conservation law enforcement strengthens local governance.  

These outcomes foster long-term stewardship and reduce dependency on environmentally harmful practices.  

---

**6. Challenges and Recommendations**  
Despite successes, challenges remain:  

- **Funding continuity**: Many projects rely on short-term grants; sustained financing is needed for ongoing maintenance.  
- **Climate variability**: Rising sea levels and extreme weather events can damage young plantations.  
- **Land tenure conflicts**: Clear legal frameworks are essential to prevent encroachment and ensure community rights.  

Recommendations include integrating mangrove restoration into national climate adaptation plans, expanding community-led initiatives, and enhancing cross-border cooperation for species and habitat protection.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Coastal mangrove restoration in Southeast Asia delivers substantial benefits for biodiversity conservation, carbon sequestration, and community livelihoods. Continued investment in science-based restoration techniques, combined with local engagement, can strengthen resilience against climate change and secure the ecological integrity of these vital ecosystems.  

---

[2] Friess, D.A., et al. (2019). The state of the world’s mangrove forests: Past, present, and future. *Annual Review of Environment and Resources*, 44, 89–115.
