# Use of Grey Water and Recycled Water for Irrigation As drought conditions become increasingly likely over time, it’s essential that we all learn to use water more efficiently. Using grey water or recycled water can help to conserve our finite water resources. # ABOUT GREY WATER Grey water is untreated, non-disinfected household wastewater that does not include toilet waste. It may be sourced from showers, baths, and washing machines. # WHEN CAN GREY WATER BE USED? Grey water can be safely used to water landscape plants and orchard trees. In California, washing machine systems that do not alter the house plumbing can be built without a construction permit as long as certain guidelines are followed, detailed here: https://greywateraction.org/greywater-reuse/. In a typical laundryto-landscape system, the water should enter the landscape at the dripline of plants with a good cover of mulch. The system’s discharge points themselves must be covered with a 2 inch layer of mulch, stones or a plastic shield. Grey water must not be used in a sprinkler system. # WHEN TO AVOID USING GREY WATER Because grey water can contain bacteria and viruses that cause illness, it should not be used to grow vegetables if the edible portion may come in contact with the soil. For example, grey water should not be used for growing asparagus, beets, carrots, cucumbers, lettuces and other salad greens, garlic, onions, potatoes, melons, squash, bush beans, radish, turnip, unstaked tomatoes, or strawberries. In contrast, recycled water, discussed later, has been disinfected, making it safe for such crops. # CHOOSING GREY WATER-COMPATIBLE HOUSEHOLD PRODUCTS When using laundry rinse water to irrigate plants, your choice of household products will affect the composition of the grey water. The wrong products can adversely affect plants and soils. It is best to avoid using products that contain sodium or sodium compounds, bleach, and/or boron, as these can result in an alkaline soil condition that suppresses healthy soil biologic activity and is poorly tolerated by many plants. Although the UC Master Gardener Program of Contra Costa County cannot recommend any particular products, the FAQ page on Greywater Action’s website ( https://greywateraction.org/greywater-faq/) lists some products that are plant-friendly. These are generally biodegradable, non-toxic, salt-free and boronfree, including products from Oasis, ECOS, Vaska and others. The Ecology Center in Berkeley has also evaluated a number of cleaning products for compatibility with greywater systems; they also recommend products from Oasis, ECOS, and other brands. Consult their website at https://ecologycenter.org/factsheets/ for a current list of products. (Click on link to Greywater Compatible Cleaning Products). # SALT & BORON TOLERANT PLANTS: If you are not able to use products with low sodium and/or low boron levels, using grey water can adversely impact many landscape plants. However, several websites provide information on plants that can tolerate higher-than-normal levels of salts and boron: http://www.fao.org/docrep/003/T0234E/T0234E05.htm#ch4.1.3 http://slosson.ucdavis.edu/Landscape\_Plant\_Selection\_Guide\_for\_Recycled\_Water\_Irrigation/ Additional lists of salt- and boron-tolerant landscape plants can be found in the University of California reference book entitled Abiotic Disorders of Landscape Plants. Low tolerance indicates plants that prefer boron levels no greater than $\\mathbf { 0.5 ^ { - 1 . 0 } m g / l }$ . Moderate-tolerance plants can manage a range of $\\mathbf { 1.0 { - 2 . 0 } \ m g / l }$ . High-tolerance plants should tolerate levels in the $\\mathbf { 2.0 { - 1 0 . 0 } \ m g / l }$ range. This reference book can be purchased online or at book stores, or it may be available at your local public library. To purchase online, visit: https://anrcatalog.ucanr.edu/Details.aspx?itemNo=3420. # ABOUT RECYCLED WATER According to the California Department of Water Resources, recycled water is “highly treated wastewater from various sources such as domestic sewage, industrial wastewater and storm water runoff.” This water has been through three levels of treatment including filtration and disinfection. # WHEN CAN RECYCLED WATER BE USED? Recycled (or reclaimed) water has been safely used for irrigation for many years, is carefully regulated in California, and can be delivered to plants by either drip or sprinkler irrigation methods. It can be safely used to water trees, gardens, vegetables and lawns. All fruits, vegetables, and herbs should be thoroughly washed with drinking water prior to consuming them. Recycled water should not be used for drinking, cooking, bathing or showering.

**The Charm of Yesterday’s Playgrounds: Why Vintage Designs Deserve a Comeback**  

It’s hard to walk past a modern playground without noticing the dominance of plastic structures, muted color palettes, and standardized modular designs. While these spaces are often built with safety and durability in mind, they lack the distinctive personality that once defined neighborhood play areas in the mid-20th century. The playgrounds of the 1950s were not just functional—they were expressions of community identity, artistry, and imagination. As cities and towns explore ways to revitalize public spaces, revisiting vintage playground aesthetics could offer both emotional and practical benefits.  

**Aesthetic Appeal Rooted in Craftsmanship**  
One of the most striking features of 1950s playgrounds was their use of wrought iron. Slides gleamed under the sun, their curving forms both inviting and sculptural. Climbing frames were often painted in vibrant primary colors, creating a joyful visual presence even from a distance. These structures weren’t simply assembled from prefabricated kits; they were often crafted locally, allowing for unique flourishes and designs that reflected the character of the community.  

Sand pits, too, held a special place in these playgrounds. They provided open-ended play where children could dig, build, and imagine, unconstrained by rigid forms. Today, such elements are often omitted or replaced by rubber flooring, which—while safer in some respects—removes the tactile variety that once made playgrounds such rich sensory environments.  

**Nostalgia as a Community Asset**  
Reviving vintage designs isn’t just about aesthetics—it’s about reconnecting with shared memories. Many adults today can recall the thrill of climbing a tall metal frame, the heat of the slide on a summer afternoon, or the gritty texture of sand between their fingers. These experiences form a collective nostalgia that cities can tap into to foster community engagement.  

Restored or newly built playgrounds in the vintage style could serve as living monuments to local history. Imagine a neighborhood fundraiser to refurbish an old iron swing set, or a community art project to repaint climbing frames in period-accurate hues. Such initiatives strengthen bonds between generations: grandparents can share stories of their own childhoods while watching their grandchildren play on similar equipment.  

**Safety in the Modern Era**  
Of course, any revival must take into account current safety standards. The 1950s playgrounds, while charming, often lacked protective surfacing and sometimes featured heights or designs that posed risks. Modern materials and engineering can preserve the look while improving safety. For example, wrought iron frames can be rebuilt with rounded edges and non-toxic coatings, slides can be designed with gentler slopes, and sand pits can be maintained with regular cleaning to ensure hygiene.  

The challenge lies in balancing authenticity with responsible design. It’s possible to create equipment that captures the essence of vintage playgrounds without replicating hazards. Advances in metallurgy, powder coating, and cushioning surfaces mean that a 1950s-inspired playground can meet rigorous safety codes while retaining its nostalgic appeal.  

**A Vision for Future Public Spaces**  
In an age when urban planning often emphasizes uniformity and cost-efficiency, vintage-inspired playgrounds offer an opportunity to stand out. They can become focal points for parks, drawing visitors not only for play but for photography, community events, and even tourism. Towns that invest in such designs signal a commitment to cultural heritage, creativity, and human-scale environments.  

The revival of these playgrounds also aligns with broader movements toward placemaking—creating spaces where people feel a sense of belonging and pride. By reintroducing wrought-iron slides, colorful climbing frames, and sand pits, municipalities can craft environments that are both playful and meaningful.  

**Conclusion**  
The playgrounds of the 1950s embodied more than just a place for children to burn energy. They were works of art, social hubs, and markers of local craftsmanship. A thoughtful revival of these designs could bring back the vibrancy, individuality, and emotional resonance that many modern playgrounds lack. With careful attention to safety and community involvement, vintage playgrounds can once again become cherished landmarks—bridging the past and present in joyful, tangible ways.

**Community Recycling Goes Green: Renewable Energy Powers Local Waste Solutions**  

In towns and neighborhoods across the country, a new wave of community-based recycling initiatives is taking root—combining grassroots engagement with cutting-edge renewable energy systems to turn household waste into reusable consumer goods. These projects are redefining the traditional recycling model by embedding sustainability into every stage of the process, from waste collection to product manufacturing.  

**A New Model for Local Waste Management**  

Unlike large-scale municipal recycling plants that often rely on conventional energy sources, these community-led operations are powered entirely by renewable technologies such as solar arrays, small wind turbines, and biomass generators. Facilities are typically modest in scale, designed to handle the waste streams of a single community or district. This keeps transportation distances minimal, reducing emissions, and ensures that local residents have a direct stake in the operation’s success.  

The approach is twofold: first, to process recyclable materials using clean energy, and second, to convert these materials into practical, marketable goods that can be sold or distributed locally. Common outputs include recycled-plastic household items, upcycled furniture, and construction materials made from compressed waste composites. These goods often replace imports from outside the community, strengthening local economies while reducing the environmental footprint of production.  

**Social Engagement as a Driving Force**  

Organizers stress that social participation is as important as the technology itself. Many projects begin with workshops and community meetings to educate residents about waste separation, the environmental benefits of renewables, and the economic potential of localized recycling. Volunteers often help operate collection points, sort materials, and even participate in small-scale manufacturing.  

In one coastal town, a solar-powered recycling hub has become a focal point for civic pride. Residents bring sorted waste to the facility, where it is weighed and logged. In return, participants receive credits redeemable for locally produced goods. This feedback loop not only incentivizes proper waste management but also keeps the value generated by the facility circulating within the community.  

**Logistics and Waste Stream Management**  

Efficient waste stream logistics are crucial to the success of these projects. Organizers have found that mapping the flow of materials—from households to the processing facility—helps identify bottlenecks and opportunities for improvement. Many initiatives deploy electric cargo bikes or small renewable-powered vehicles for collection, ensuring that transportation aligns with the overall sustainability goals.  

Once materials arrive at the facility, renewable-powered shredders, compactors, and extrusion machines take over. Solar furnaces, for example, can melt metals for reuse, while wind-powered grinders reduce glass into cullet for remanufacturing. Because these machines operate on clean energy, the carbon footprint of the recycling process is significantly lower than that of conventional plants.  

**Economic and Environmental Impact**  

Early data from pilot programs suggest that renewable-powered recycling facilities can achieve notable reductions in greenhouse gas emissions while fostering local job creation. By transforming waste into goods for local markets, communities also retain more economic value internally. This model reduces dependency on external supply chains and mitigates the environmental costs associated with long-distance transportation of both raw materials and finished products.  

Moreover, the visibility of these projects—often located in central, accessible areas—helps normalize sustainable practices. Residents can see firsthand how waste is converted into new products, reinforcing the message that resource recovery is both practical and beneficial.  

**Looking Ahead**  

As renewable energy technologies become more affordable and accessible, experts predict that community-based recycling powered by clean energy will expand rapidly. Partnerships between local governments, non-profits, and renewable technology providers are emerging to support the establishment of these facilities in diverse regions, from rural villages to urban neighborhoods.  

The model’s strength lies in its integration of environmental responsibility, economic resilience, and civic engagement. By harnessing renewable energy to process and repurpose household waste, communities are not only reducing their ecological footprint but also building stronger, more self-sufficient local economies.  

In the coming years, observers expect these initiatives to serve as templates for sustainable development worldwide—proving that with the right blend of technology and community spirit, waste can truly become a resource.

**Crafting Wood Furniture by Hand: A Guide to Sustainable Practices**  

For those who appreciate the warmth, durability, and character of wood furniture, handcrafting pieces offers not only creative satisfaction but also the opportunity to make environmentally conscious choices. By focusing on sustainable timber selection, traditional joinery, and natural finishing methods, you can create furniture that stands the test of time while minimizing waste and reducing your ecological footprint.  

---

### Choosing Sustainable Timber Species  

The foundation of any woodworking project begins with the choice of timber. Opting for sustainably sourced wood ensures that your materials are harvested in ways that maintain forest health and biodiversity. Look for certifications such as FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) or PEFC (Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification), which indicate responsible forestry practices.  

Native and locally grown species often have a lower transportation footprint and can be just as beautiful and durable as exotic woods. Hardwoods like oak, maple, and walnut offer longevity and strength, while softwoods such as pine and cedar provide lighter weight and a distinctive grain pattern. When possible, reclaim wood from old buildings, pallets, or discarded furniture to give it new life—reducing demand for freshly cut timber and preserving natural resources.  

---

### Employing Traditional Joinery Techniques  

Modern woodworking often relies on screws, nails, and synthetic adhesives, but traditional joinery techniques can enhance both the aesthetic and structural integrity of a piece. Mortise and tenon joints, dovetails, and lap joints are examples of methods that use precise cuts and interlocking shapes to create strong connections without excessive hardware.  

These techniques require patience and skill, but they eliminate the need for many synthetic materials and can make repairs easier in the future. A well-executed joint not only improves durability but also tells a story of craftsmanship—a connection between the maker and the material that is often lost in mass production.  

---

### Finishing with Natural Oils and Waxes  

The finishing process protects wood surfaces from wear, moisture, and stains while enhancing their natural beauty. Many commercial finishes contain solvents and synthetic chemicals that can release harmful VOCs (volatile organic compounds) into the environment.  

Natural alternatives such as tung oil, linseed oil, and beeswax provide effective protection without introducing unnecessary toxins. These finishes penetrate the wood, highlighting grain patterns and imparting a warm, organic sheen. They are also easy to reapply over time, allowing the furniture to age gracefully and remain functional for decades.  

---

### Reducing Waste in the Workshop  

Sustainability in woodworking extends beyond the choice of materials. Efficient planning, precise measuring, and careful cutting help minimize offcuts and scrap. Smaller pieces of leftover wood can be repurposed into accessories like coasters, picture frames, or decorative trim. Sawdust can be composted or used as mulch in gardens, turning what would be waste into a resource.  

Organizing your workspace to store reusable materials and maintaining tools properly will also reduce the need for replacements and additional purchases. By viewing each project as part of a larger cycle of use and reuse, you create a workshop culture that values conservation as much as creativity.  

---

### Embracing Longevity and Repair  

The most sustainable piece of furniture is one that remains in use for generations. Designing with durability in mind—solid joints, quality finishes, and thoughtful proportions—ensures that your work will withstand daily wear. Additionally, creating furniture that can be easily repaired or refinished extends its life and keeps it out of landfills.  

Furniture that is adaptable, such as modular shelving or tables with adjustable heights, can evolve with changing needs, reducing the likelihood of disposal. This approach fosters a deep connection between maker, owner, and object, encouraging care and maintenance rather than replacement.  

---

**Conclusion**  

Handcrafting wood furniture offers a unique opportunity to merge artistry with environmental stewardship. By choosing sustainable timber, embracing traditional joinery, finishing with natural oils, and committing to waste reduction, each project becomes part of a broader effort to preserve resources and celebrate craftsmanship. The pieces you create will not only serve functional purposes but also stand as enduring symbols of thoughtful, responsible making.

**Retail Sector Embraces Eco-Friendly Gift Cards to Cut Single-Use Plastics**  

*By Staff Writer*  

In a bid to reduce environmental impact and align with growing consumer demand for sustainable products, a number of major retailers are switching from traditional PVC-based gift cards to eco-friendly alternatives made from biodegradable or recycled materials. This shift reflects a broader trend in the retail industry toward reducing single-use plastics and promoting more responsible resource use.  

**From PVC to Plant-Based and Recycled Materials**  

For decades, most gift cards have been manufactured from polyvinyl chloride (PVC), a durable plastic that is inexpensive to produce but problematic in terms of disposal. PVC is not biodegradable and can release harmful chemicals during production and incineration. In response to mounting concerns over plastic pollution, manufacturers have developed new materials such as polylactic acid (PLA), derived from corn starch or sugarcane, and PETG or rPET, which are made from recycled plastic bottles.  

These alternatives can significantly reduce the environmental footprint of gift cards. PLA, for instance, is compostable under industrial conditions, breaking down into natural components without leaving microplastics. Recycled PET options extend the life cycle of existing materials, diverting waste from landfills and reducing the need for virgin plastic production.  

**Retailers Leading the Change**  

Several global and regional retailers have announced commitments to phase out PVC gift cards entirely. Large department stores, grocery chains, and specialty retailers are working with card manufacturers to ensure that their new eco-friendly cards meet durability and security standards while offering the same convenience to customers.  

In some cases, retailers are also introducing digital gift cards as part of their sustainability push. By offering a mobile or email-based option, companies can eliminate physical materials altogether, appealing to tech-savvy consumers and reducing shipping-related emissions.  

**Impact on Single-Use Plastic Reduction**  

The transition to biodegradable and recycled gift cards represents a tangible step toward reducing single-use plastics in the retail sector. While gift cards may seem small compared to other packaging and product components, their widespread use—often in large quantities during peak shopping seasons—means that switching materials can have a meaningful cumulative effect.  

Industry analysts note that the move could influence other areas of retail operations, encouraging companies to reconsider materials used in loyalty cards, membership cards, and promotional items. As consumer awareness grows, retailers that proactively adopt sustainable materials may benefit from enhanced brand reputation and increased customer loyalty.  

**Challenges and Considerations**  

Despite the promise of eco-friendly gift cards, there are challenges to widespread adoption. PLA cards, for example, require specific composting facilities to break down effectively, and such infrastructure is not universally available. Recycled PET cards still rely on plastic, albeit repurposed, and must be carefully managed at end-of-life to ensure they do not contribute to further pollution.  

Cost is another factor. Sustainable materials can be more expensive to source and produce, particularly at smaller scales. Retailers must weigh these costs against potential marketing and reputational benefits, as well as the long-term savings associated with reduced environmental impact.  

**Consumer Response**  

Early feedback from shoppers has been largely positive, with many expressing appreciation for the effort to reduce plastic waste. Some retailers are using in-store signage and online campaigns to highlight the environmental benefits of their new gift cards, turning the change into an opportunity for customer engagement.  

Experts suggest that clear communication is key to ensuring that eco-friendly cards are disposed of properly. For biodegradable materials, instructions on composting or recycling can help prevent them from ending up in conventional waste streams where their advantages are lost.  

**Looking Ahead**  

The adoption of biodegradable and recycled gift cards is part of a wider movement in retail toward sustainable practices. As technology improves and economies of scale drive down costs, more retailers are expected to join the trend, potentially making eco-friendly gift cards the industry standard within the next decade.  

In combination with other measures—such as reducing packaging, sourcing renewable energy for operations, and expanding product recycling programs—these initiatives underscore the retail sector’s evolving role in addressing environmental challenges. For consumers, the shift offers a tangible reminder that everyday purchases, even something as small as a gift card, can contribute to a larger effort to reduce single-use plastics and protect the planet’s resources.

**Bright Ideas for Lowering Household Energy Costs**  

In an era of rising utility bills and increasing environmental awareness, finding practical ways to reduce household energy consumption has become a priority for many. While large-scale changes such as installing solar panels or upgrading to energy-efficient appliances can be impactful, there are also smaller, cost-effective methods that can deliver meaningful savings over time. Three of the most effective strategies include switching to LED lightbulbs, using programmable thermostats, and improving home insulation.  

### Switching to LED Lightbulbs  

Lighting accounts for a notable portion of household electricity usage, and traditional incandescent bulbs are notoriously inefficient. LED (light-emitting diode) bulbs provide a powerful alternative. They use up to 80% less energy than incandescent lighting and can last 15 to 25 times longer. This longevity not only reduces the frequency of replacements but also lowers the overall cost of lighting over the lifespan of the bulb.  

LEDs are available in a range of brightness levels and color temperatures, making them suitable for every space—from warm, ambient lighting in bedrooms to bright, daylight tones in kitchens and work areas. Additionally, their instant-on capability and compatibility with dimmer switches offer flexibility for both energy savings and comfort. By gradually replacing existing bulbs with LEDs, households can quickly see a drop in electricity consumption without compromising on light quality.  

### Using Programmable Thermostats  

Heating and cooling systems are often the largest contributors to home energy use. A programmable thermostat allows homeowners to fine-tune indoor temperatures according to daily routines. For example, the thermostat can be set to lower heating output during the night or when no one is home, and then return to a comfortable temperature just before occupants arrive.  

Modern programmable models often include “smart” features, such as learning user habits, remote adjustments via smartphone apps, and integration with other energy-saving devices. By avoiding unnecessary heating and cooling, households can reduce energy waste significantly. Even modest adjustments—such as lowering the heat by 2–3 degrees in winter or raising the cooling temperature slightly in summer—can translate into measurable cost savings over time.  

### Improving Home Insulation  

No matter how efficient a heating or cooling system is, much of its energy can be lost if a home is poorly insulated. Insulation acts as a barrier to heat transfer, keeping warm air inside during winter and cool air inside during summer. Common points of energy leakage include attics, walls, floors, and around windows and doors.  

Upgrading insulation materials in key areas can lead to dramatic efficiency gains. In older homes, adding insulation to the attic or replacing worn weatherstripping can be a relatively low-cost project with high returns. For newer homes, ensuring that insulation meets or exceeds current energy codes can help maintain energy efficiency over decades.  

Even small improvements, such as sealing gaps around window frames or installing insulated curtains, can contribute to better temperature control and reduced reliance on heating and cooling systems. Combined with other strategies, insulation upgrades often pay for themselves within a few years through lower utility bills.  

### Putting It All Together  

These three measures—LED lighting, programmable thermostats, and improved insulation—address different aspects of household energy use, from lighting to temperature management to structural efficiency. Implementing them does not require major renovations or investments, and each offers both immediate and long-term benefits.  

Households that adopt these strategies often find that energy savings accumulate month after month, leading to lower bills and a smaller environmental footprint. Moreover, these steps can be tailored to specific needs: some may start with lighting upgrades, while others focus on thermostat programming or insulation improvements.  

By taking a thoughtful, step-by-step approach, homeowners can create an energy-efficient living environment that is both comfortable and cost-effective. In the process, they contribute to a broader effort to conserve resources and promote sustainable living—one practical change at a time.
